case_studies.name: DecoBrush: Drawing Structured Decorative Patterns by Example (Lu, Barnes, Wan, Asente, Měch, Finkelstein, SIGGRAPH 2014)
case_studies.what_it_is: An example-based 'decorative brush': the designer supplies a library of 8-12 exemplar flourish strokes in one consistent style and sketches a path, and the system synthesises a new flourish in that style following the path.
case_studies.how_it_works: Offline: exemplars are rasterised (optionally as a signed distance field). For each, the user marks the start and end of the main branch; a smooth spine is found by Dijkstra on the pixel grid following edge-tangent flow, then a quartic fit, and the stroke gets a uv parameterisation (30-100 samples of spine, left and right outline). Runtime: (1) piecewise matching of the query path to exemplar segments by dynamic programming over features (turning angle, width, distance to ends), heavily penalising stroke ends matched to exemplar middles, since curls at stroke ends carry the style; (2) as-rigid-as-possible deformation of the matched segments onto the query spine; (3) graph-cut seams where segments overlap; (4) hierarchical patch-based texture synthesis to repair distortion and add structural variation; (5) vectorise (they used Illustrator).
case_studies.relevance: A 'by example' alternative to rule writing, aimed at designers. The style lives in the drawn library, and the dominant curve is the sketched path. Its pipeline is raster-based, though, which conflicts with crisp, mathematically exact engraved lines.
borrowable_ideas: A style library of 8-12 consistent exemplar strokes drawn by the designer, each with an explicit spine and treated ends.
Dynamic-programming segment assignment along a dominant curve: choose which pre-drawn flourish segments cover which stretch, with costs that protect terminal curls from being cut.
ARAP rather than plain bending when mapping exemplar segments, to keep leaf and curl shapes from shearing.
Treat stroke terminals (curls, buds) as protected style features, consistent with skeletal-stroke anchoring.
case_studies.designer_workflow: Very approachable: choose a library and draw a path, with refinement by brush/eraser strokes. Downsides for this project: raster synthesis, then vectorisation, means outlines are approximations, not the exact φ-governed geometry the user wants.
case_studies.evidence: Opened the Princeton PDF and read the extracted introduction, related work, exemplar processing and synthesis sections (4-5).

case_studies.name: Owen Jones, The Grammar of Ornament (1856): General Principles (37 propositions) and chapter analyses
case_studies.what_it_is: The Victorian rulebook of ornament. The propositions at the front state the structural laws the user is reaching for, and the chapter texts restate them as principles observed in Greek, Moresque, Chinese and other ornament.
case_studies.how_it_works: Relevant propositions (wording from readingdesign.org transcription): 6, beauty of form comes from lines growing out of one another in gradual undulations, with no excrescences; 7, general forms first, then subdivision by general lines, then filling the interstices, which may again be subdivided 'for closer inspection'; 8, all ornament should be based on a geometrical construction; 9, every assemblage should be arranged on definite proportions, 'those proportions will be the most beautiful which it will be most difficult for the eye to detect', e.g. 5:8 better than 4:8, 3:7 than 3:6; 10, harmony of form is the proper balancing and contrast of the straight, the inclined and the curved; 11, all lines should flow out of a parent stem, every ornament traceable to its branch and root; 12, all junctions of curved with curved or curved with straight should be tangential; 13, use conventionalised, not literal, natural forms. Greek chapter (Ch. IV) names the trio: radiation from the parent stem, proportionate distribution of the areas, and tangential curvature of the lines. It also notes that in Byzantine, Arabian/Moresque and Early English styles the flowers flow off on either side from a continuous line. Moresque chapter: ornament flows off from a parent stem; division and subdivision of general lines; lines in equilibrium of straight, inclined and curved; Alhambra patterns arise from intersections of equidistant lines round fixed centres. Chinese chapter: floral patterns obey radiation from the parent stem and tangential curvature.
case_studies.relevance: Supplies the 'grammar' the engine should enforce as hard constraints and lint rules: hierarchy (parent stem), tangency, top-down subdivision, geometric basis, and subtle proportion. Prop. 9's 5:8 is a Fibonacci approximation of φ.
borrowable_ideas: Hard constraint: every element has a path of parent links back to a root dominant curve (Prop. 11). The engine refuses orphan geometry.
Hard constraint: every junction is tangential (Prop. 12). Children start with the parent's tangent; ideally match curvature too.

Pipeline order mirrors Prop. 7: general forms (page frame, dominant curves), then general lines (scroll spines), then interstices (leaves, fillers), then fine enrichment (hatching) that only appears at close inspection or high zoom.
Proportion system from Prop. 9: one recurring ratio set (φ and its Fibonacci approximants 5:8, 8:13), applied to panel areas and element lengths, never 1:2 halves.
'Radiation from the parent stem': leaves on a scroll emanate from it in a regular angular or arc-length progression rather than being scattered.
Balance check from Prop. 10: track proportions of straight (frame rules), inclined (lattice, zigzag) and curved (scrolls) line length per region.
case_studies.designer_workflow: These are rules a designer already intuits. Encoding them as automatic checks with visual flags (non-tangent junction, orphan element, constant-curvature run, ratio off target) lets the user draw freely while the engine enforces the grammar.
case_studies.evidence: Opened readingdesign.org's transcription of propositions 1-14. Opened the archive.org djvu full text of the 1868 edition and read summaries of the General Principles, Ch. IV Greek, the end of the Moresque chapter and the Chinese chapter (characters 0-100k and 200k-300k).

case_studies.name: Lewis F. Day (The Anatomy of Pattern 1887; Nature in Ornament 1892) and Christopher Dresser (Principles of Decorative Design 1873) on skeletons, growth lines, curves and proportion
case_studies.what_it_is: Victorian design-teaching texts that describe ornament as foliage clothing a structural skeleton, and that rank curves and proportions.
case_studies.how_it_works: Day, Anatomy of Pattern: ornament is built on lines inevitable to its consistency, which serve as 'the skeleton or framework upon which you build up your pattern'. Hiding the scaffolding does not remove the construction. 'Pattern is a vertebrate thing; in a scroll the spinal cord is very decidedly pronounced'. The best way to disguise the skeleton is to clothe it, as nature does. 'The spiral itself is only a series of segments of circles' (compass practice). 'You cannot draw a bold, flowing scroll without considerable allowance in the way of length'. Designs must be shaped to a rectangular plan of fixed dimensions. Day, Nature in Ornament (https://archive.org/stream/cu31924031243763/cu31924031243763_djvu.txt): a stem has no business to grow two ways at once; 'a formal arrangement of lines involves an equally formal kind of foliation'; medieval leaves were designed into set spaces (square, diamond, circle, vesica). Day also values the natural line over the mechanical, and warns that distributing detail according to a diagram is not designing. He notes that the thickening of the leaf-stalk where it joins the stem is rarely used. Dresser (https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/39749/pg39749.txt): the arc is the least beautiful curve, the ellipse (two centres) is better, the egg curve (three centres) better still. As the number of centres needed grows, the curve's origin becomes harder to detect. Proportion must be subtle; a surface should never be divided into halves; 3:8, 5:8 and 5:13 are good (Fibonacci approximants of φ and φ²; he does not name the golden section in the portion read).
case_studies.relevance: Direct historical justification for the user's architecture: dominant 'vertebrate' curves with relative foliage. Also for curvature-varying curves and φ-like proportions. Day's warnings define the 'mechanical' failure mode to avoid.
borrowable_ideas: Name the engine's core object a Skeleton/Spine. Foliage is always 'clothing' attached to it, and the skeleton can be shown or hidden as a debug layer.
Consistency rule (Day): the formality of the foliage follows the formality of its dominant curve. Golden-spiral scrolls get strictly self-similar leaves, while freer curves allow more variation.
No two-way growth: each scroll has a growth direction (base to tip), and leaf scale and orientation are monotone along it.
Curvature quality metric (Dresser/Ruskin): penalise long constant-curvature runs. If spirals are built from compass arcs (Day), make that an explicit, chosen style and keep radii in φ progression.
Length budget (Day): a scroll period needs a minimum length, so at small page sizes reduce the number of scroll periods rather than compressing them.
Leaf-stalk swell at the junction with the stem, as a width-profile detail that strengthens the tangential junction visually.
case_studies.designer_workflow: These books were written to teach designers to plan the skeleton first, then clothe it. That is the workflow the engine should impose: the designer draws or chooses dominant curves, then assigns foliage libraries to them.

Quotes are from these public-domain texts as returned by the fetch tool.

case_studies.name: Designer-control research: Gieseke et al. 'Organized Order in Ornamentation' (CAe 2017) and 'A Survey of Control Mechanisms for Creative Pattern Generation' (CGF 2021); PATEX (Guerrero et al. 2016)
case_studies.what_it_is: Work on how artists can steer ornament and pattern generators. A 2017 system of combinable placement functions, a 2021 survey classifying control mechanisms, and PATEX, which proposes alternative regularity interpretations as edit suggestions.
case_studies.how_it_works: From abstracts only. Gieseke 2017 fills space automatically with modular, combinable element placement functions under global constraints (balanced distribution, symmetry). Drawn strokes define connections and hierarchy, user-drawn guides define vector fields that ornament follows as streamlines, path planning routes ornament around obstacles and aligns it to their borders, and individual accent elements are placed by hand. The 2021 survey organises techniques by design feature (repetition, frames, curves, directionality, visual accents) and by input mode (exemplars, parameterisation, handling, filling, guiding, placing). PATEX detects multiple valid readings of a pattern's regularity (symmetry, spacing, alignment) and offers them as suggested edits, using a linear approximation to keep the search tractable.
case_studies.relevance: Supports a mixed-initiative design: the engine fills and balances, the designer guides and places accents, and relationships are preserved during edits.
borrowable_ideas: Separate 'guiding' inputs (dominant curves, fields) from 'placing' inputs (accent elements like the crest, jewel pendant and cartouche) and from 'filling' (automatic leaves and fillers).
Placement functions as composable TS functions (e.g. along(curve, spacing) ∘ mirror(axis) ∘ scaleBy(φ)), so a layout is a readable expression rather than a hand-placed list.
When the designer moves one element, offer relationship-preserving variants (keep the mirror, keep φ spacing) instead of silently breaking constraints.
case_studies.designer_workflow: Explicitly artist-centred. Key lesson: give high-level guiding and filling controls and low-level accent placement, not parameter soup.
case_studies.evidence: Did not open the full papers: the Purdue survey PDF exceeded the fetch size limit and the EG digital library returned 403 or refused the connection. The 2017 and 2021 details come from abstracts in search results, plus the Purdue publication page (bibliographic data only). Opened the PATEX project page (abstract).

principles.principle: Parent stem: every element descends from a dominant curve; no orphan geometry.
principles.source: Owen Jones Prop. 11 and Greek/Moresque chapters; Wong et al. element tree; Deco Topology graph
principles.apply_how: Represent the scene as a graph: root dominant curves (page frame curves, side ribbon spines, medallion scroll spines), then children attached by (parentId, t, side, departureAngle, scale). Rendering walks the graph; an element without a parent path is a build error.

principles.principle: Tangential junction: children leave parents along the parent's tangent, ideally with matched curvature.
principles.source: Owen Jones Prop. 12; Wong et al. Sec. 2.1.3; Xu & Mould branching (children spawned on the parent path)
principles.apply_how: Construct each child curve starting from the parent's local frame at t, with initial heading = parent tangent plus a departure angle that is eased in, so curvature starts near the parent's. Lint: flag any junction whose tangent angle error exceeds about 1°.

principles.principle: Continuously varying curvature; avoid circular-arc runs.
principles.source: Ruskin as quoted by Xu & Mould; Dresser on curves with more centres; Xu & Mould magnetic curves
principles.apply_how: Define scroll and leaf curves by curvature programs κ(s): log spiral κ = 1/(b(L−s)), golden when b = 2·ln(φ)/π ≈ 0.306; magnetic or log-aesthetic exponents for softer curls. Fit these to designer-drawn Illustrator paths, then output Béziers. Lint long near-constant-curvature runs.

principles.principle: Scaled repetition by a single similarity: self-similar leaves put their tips on a golden spiral automatically.
principles.source: Wong et al. scaled repetition and equal-angle spiral pattern; Jones 'radiation from the parent stem'; derivation in this report
principles.apply_how: For the flame corner and acanthus scrolls, draw ONE leaf. Generate the rest by repeatedly applying a spiral similarity about the scroll's pole (rotate Δθ, scale φ^(−Δθ/(π/2))). Tip points then lie exactly on a golden log spiral, and each leaf's curl is a scaled copy of the golden master curl. The engine can draw that spiral as a check overlay.

principles.principle: Top-down hierarchy: general forms, then general lines, then interstices, then enrichment.
principles.source: Jones Prop. 7; Wong et al. phase gating and hierarchical subdivision; Day's skeleton first, then clothing
principles.apply_how: Fixed engine phases with per-phase rule sets: FRAME, then DOMINANT, then PRIMARY_SCROLLS, then LEAVES, then FILLERS, then HATCH/ENGRAVE. Later phases may read but never move earlier-phase geometry.

principles.principle: Balance by measured negative space (uniform density).
principles.source: Wong et al. horror vacui and largest-empty-circle heuristic; FLOWPAK balance principle and refinement; Jones 'proportionate distribution of the areas'
principles.apply_how: After each phase, compute a distance field of occupied proxies inside each panel. Use local maxima (empty circles) to drive filler growth, and report a density-variance score per panel so the designer sees imbalance numerically.

principles.principle: Even or logically graded spacing for clustered lines.
principles.source: FLOWPAK's adaptation of Jobard-Lefer streamlines (d_gap, d_stop = 0.8·d_gap)
principles.apply_how: Clustered parallel lines are offset curves or streamlines of the dominant curve's field. Their separation follows a declared rule (constant, or geometric with ratio 1/φ moving away from the dominant line), with d_stop preventing collisions where curves converge.

principles.principle: Analogy: the same rhythmic controlling line places different elements.
principles.source: Wong et al. Sec. 2.1.1 (analogy, recurrence of a ratio)
principles.apply_how: Reuse one dominant curve family (and one ratio) across medallion, flame, crest and side bands. Elements differ but share parameterisation, so the page reads as one system.

principles.principle: Fit to boundaries with integer periods, then stretch.
principles.source: Wong et al. meander-period fitting; Day on scroll length; Wackrill gcd rule for plaits
principles.apply_how: For every band and weave along a side, choose integer counts (scroll periods, crossings, beads) for the current length within allowed min/max period lengths, preferring counts that preserve topology (gcd = 1 for a single continuous ribbon). Distribute the remainder by continuous stretching of stretchable (non-anchored) parts.

principles.principle: Corners get a dedicated element.
principles.source: Wong et al. Sec. 2.1.3; Asente automatic corner tiles
principles.apply_how: The four corners are fixed anchors (medallions, flame) that dominant curves emanate from. Side bands terminate into them via generated or hand-drawn corner tiles; never let a band simply turn a sharp corner.

principles.principle: Strict alternation for interlace.
principles.source: Mercat (Klein Project); Gross & Tucker grid rule; Kaplan Taprats interlace (degree 2 or 4 vertices)
principles.apply_how: Over/under is computed from crossing parity along each strand, never stored by hand. Validate that every crossing joins exactly two strands, and re-derive after any resize or break toggle.

principles.principle: Subtle, recurring proportion; never halves.
principles.source: Jones Prop. 9 (5:8 over 4:8; proportions hardest to detect are most beautiful); Dresser (3:8, 5:8, 5:13; never divide into halves)
principles.apply_how: A global ratio palette (φ, φ², with Fibonacci approximants) used for panel splits, crest proportions and leaf length decay. Lint 1:2 splits of decorated areas.

principles.principle: Formality consistency and single growth direction.
principles.source: Day, Nature in Ornament ('formal arrangement of lines involves an equally formal kind of foliation'; stems don't grow two ways)
principles.apply_how: Each dominant curve has a declared formality level that sets allowed variation (0 = exact self-similar copies). Leaf scale, angle and spacing are monotone from base to tip.

principles.principle: Uniformity amidst variety (controlled, seeded variation).
principles.source: FLOWPAK citing Hutcheson; Wong et al. organic variation; Day on natural vs. mechanical line
principles.apply_how: Allow small, seeded, bounded deviations (leaf width ±3%, rotation ±2°) in low-formality zones only, so output looks engraved by a hand following rules rather than computed. Keep it deterministic per page size.

principles.principle: Symmetry is enforced structurally, not checked after the fact.
principles.source: Deco Symmetry module (collision removes whole orbit); Xu & Mould mirror-half construction
principles.apply_how: Mirror and rotation groups are graph nodes. Children of a symmetric parent are generated once and instanced through the transform list; rejecting one instance rejects all.

cautions: Local greedy growth does not produce elegant global composition. Wong et al. concede their largest-empty-circle driver makes 'willow' patterns jumbled and that balance and symmetry need global planning. Dominant curves must be designed (or optimised) first, with growth used only for subordinate fill.

Physics- or rule-driven curves are hard to aim. Xu & Mould report about 2 minutes of trial and error per curve, and say exact course control is the method's limitation. Use them in inverse mode (fit to designer-drawn curves) or only for secondary curls.

Good optimisers are slow: FLOWPAK takes about an hour for 50 elements, and DecoBrush relies on raster texture synthesis. Do heavy layout offline at a set of breakpoint sizes and ship baked parameters. At runtime only re-map (skeletal-stroke style) onto resized dominant curves.
DecoBrush and similar example-based systems synthesise in raster and then vectorise. That conflicts with exact φ-governed vector geometry and crisp engraved strokes.

Skeletal-stroke mapping folds art at curvature radii below half the art width, and corners leave gaps. Plan for rib-envelope folding avoidance and dedicated corner tiles. FLOWPAK simply avoided U-turns.

Interlace topology is discrete. Changing crossing counts on resize can change how many separate loops exist (gcd rule), and breaks can merge or split loops. Treat counts as discrete choices with explicit topology checks, not as a continuous stretch.

Golden-ratio myths: none of the historical sources read demand φ exactly. Jones prefers 5:8 and says the best proportions are hardest to detect; Dresser cites 3:8, 5:8, 5:13 without naming the golden section; Wong credits the recurrence of 'almost any ratio' with unifying a design. φ is a good organising choice, but its value is consistency, not magic. Do not let φ override optical judgement.

Mechanical perfection can read as dead. Day warns that distributing detail according to a diagram is not design, and prizes the natural line over the mechanical. Real engravings follow rules but have controlled variation and line-weight modulation, so build in bounded, seeded variation and width profiles.

Compass-arc spirals vs true log spirals: Day describes practical spirals as segments of circles, and the common 'golden spiral' drawing is quarter-circle arcs in golden rectangles. These have curvature jumps. Decide explicitly which construction the engine uses; mixing them causes visible kinks.

No turnkey JS/TS ornament engine was found. Deco used JavaScript but lived inside Flash and Photoshop. Taprats is Java and no longer developed. Kaplan & Cohen's Celtic system and Wong's system were C/C++ research code. Searches turned up no web reimplementation of Wong's floral method or Hankin's method, so expect to build the core yourself.

Wong et al. explicitly scoped out bands, half-open borders and strict symmetries. The user's page frame (borders plus bands) needs path-based techniques (skeletal strokes or pattern brushes, interlace graphs) in addition to region-filling growth.

Unverified items: Kaplan & Cohen's Celtic rendering details are from secondary descriptions (their PDF could not be opened), the Gieseke survey and 2017 paper were read only as abstracts, and Cromwell and Sloss were not opened. Check these before relying on specifics.

angles.summary: The defensible core of "golden ratio in ornament" is self-similarity, not the number 1.618. D'Arcy Thompson's gnomon theorem says that when a structure is built from parts that are similar and similarly placed, corresponding points (tips, bases, curl eyes) lie on logarithmic spirals. So the engine should generate leaves and curls by repeating one spiral-similarity transform (scale times rotation about a pole). "Golden" then just means fixing the scale step at phi per 90 degrees (b = ln(phi)/(pi/2) = 0.30635, pitch 17.03 degrees, 6.854x growth per turn). Sharp's table shows other phi-derived log spirals exist: phi per 54, 108 or 144 degrees, from pentagon and golden-triangle gnomons. That lets the designer pick how tight a curl is and still stay phi-derived. The empirical and historical record argues for honesty. Markowsky shows phi claims only hold within roughly 2% and that people cannot tell 1.6 from 1.7 rectangles. Sharp measured the nautilus at about 3x per turn, not 6.85x. The Renaissance Ionic volutes (Serlio, Salviati, Goldmann) are compass-built, piecewise-Archimedean arc chains, not golden spirals. Hübner (2024) found that people prefer a true golden spiral to the quarter-circle Fibonacci spiral mainly because its curvature is continuous. So what makes ornament read as "printed" is exact repetition under one transform plus curvature continuity (Euler-spiral easements, log-aesthetic curves), not phi to five decimals. For the designer, the workable pattern has three parts. First, a few named parameters (pole, growth rule, angular step, entry tangent and curvature). Second, on-curve authoring in the style of Spiro rather than Bezier handles. Third, a fit, report and snap loop that takes their Illustrator tracing, measures how close it is to golden and corrects it inside a stated tolerance. A conformal "design flat, wrap into spiral" mapping (z = exp(w), as in de Smit and Lenstra's analysis of Escher) is a strong way to let one master leaf be drawn once and stamped through a scroll.

case_studies.name: D'Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1917): gnomon theorem and the theory of transformations
case_studies.what_it_is: The classic morphology text. It has a chapter on the equiangular (logarithmic) spiral, a chapter on phyllotaxis, and Chapter XVII 'On the Theory of Transformations', which compares related forms by deforming a coordinate grid.
case_studies.how_it_works: Gnomon idea, from Hero and Aristotle: a gnomon is a figure that, added to a shape, leaves the result similar to the original. Thompson states three propositions. (1) If a growing structure is built of successive parts that are similar and similarly situated, log spirals can always be traced through corresponding points. (2) In horns, shells and other organic log-spiral forms, each growth increment is a gnomon to the whole existing structure. (3) Conversely, many gnomonic figures can be inscribed in a spiral by accident. Adding gnomons in succession to a 36-72-72 triangle puts its apices on a log spiral; the same holds for squares, right triangles and hexagons. Corollary: do not expect log spirals in structures whose parts form at the same time, such as a leaf margin. Look for them where growth is accretive. Transformations chapter: inscribe a form in Cartesian coordinates, deform the grid (shear, change the x/y ratio, or substitute other functions), and the figure follows the deformation 'under strain', like a map projection. He limits this to simple, harmonious transformations. The phyllotaxis chapter is skeptical. Close Fibonacci divergences are rare, while 1/2, 2/3 and 3/5 are common. The golden angle is most equable only if all leaves are crushed into a single ring, and he rejects 'ideal angle' teleology.
case_studies.relevance: This is the mathematical license for the owner's request. If every leaf of the flame is the previous leaf scaled and rotated by one fixed similarity about a pole, the curve through the leaf tips is necessarily a log spiral, and golden if the scale per 90 degrees is phi. The transformations chapter is the precedent for defining ornament in a canonical frame and mapping it onto dominant page curves.
borrowable_ideas: Leaf instancing by a repeated spiral similarity. Leaf_k = O + c^k (Leaf_0 - O) over complex coordinates, with c = s*e^{i*dTheta}. Tips, bases and vein ends then all lie on log spirals with pole O, and they are golden when s = phi^(dTheta/90deg).
Treat 'stem spiral' (through leaf bases) and 'envelope spiral' (through tips) as rotated copies of one spiral about the same pole. Their ratio is constant, so every leaf has the same aspect.

Use log spirals for accretive parts (curls, stems, chains of diminishing leaves) and other fair curves (Euler or log-aesthetic) for blade outlines. That follows Thompson's corollary that simultaneously formed margins are not spirals.
A 'coordinate-strain' layer. The designer draws a motif on a unit grid and the engine maps the grid onto a curved frame region with a simple, documented transformation.
case_studies.evidence: Downloaded the Project Gutenberg plain text (55264.txt.utf-8). Read the gnomon passage (book pp. 509-515: Figs 249-260 and the three propositions), the opening of Chapter XVII on transformations, and the end of Chapter XIV on phyllotaxis, including the Fibonacci skepticism and Sachs quote.

case_studies.name: Theodore Andrea Cook, The Curves of Life (1914)
case_studies.what_it_is: An Edwardian survey of spiral formations in nature and art, with a focus on Leonardo. It is the book where the symbol phi for the golden ratio was introduced, at Mark Barr's suggestion.
case_studies.how_it_works: Cook (p. 420) records that Mark Barr suggested calling the ratio phi, after Pheidias. He presents the phi series as a 'double Fibonacci series' with exact powers (phi^2 = 1 + phi, phi^3 = 1 + 2phi, ...). He gives Church's 'ideal angle' of 137 deg 30' 27.95" as 2*pi/phi^2. His central thesis argues against strict mathematical conformity. He criticises Colman for treating departures from 'extreme and mean proportion' as negligible, and says that life and beauty are always accompanied by deviations from any simple mathematical expression. For him mathematics is the instrument against which those deviations become measurable. He also reprints a reader's rebuttal (the Giotto's-circle letter): we admire near-exactness for the skill involved, not because it misses perfection.
case_studies.relevance: This is the historical origin of the phi vocabulary, and the first serious argument about strict phi versus deliberate deviation. That is exactly the tension in 'make it look printed and mathematically exact' versus 'make it look natural'.
borrowable_ideas: Make the dominant function the reference and record any deliberate deviation as a named, stored offset (for example 'tip 3 pushed out 4% from the golden envelope'). Do not add random jitter. That keeps the printed precision while allowing Cook's 'subtle deviation'.
Compute and show a deviation report: measured ratio versus the phi reference for each element. The math becomes a gauge rather than a straitjacket.
Use the exact identities phi^n = F(n-1) + F(n)*phi to build scales of related lengths (a phi length palette).
case_studies.evidence: Downloaded the archive.org OCR text (cu31924028937179_djvu.txt). Read p. 420 (Barr naming phi, the double Fibonacci series, the 2pi/phi^2 ideal angle), the passage critiquing Colman about deviations, and the 'Slight Divergencies and Subtle Deviations' letter.

case_studies.name: George Markowsky, 'Misconceptions about the Golden Ratio', College Mathematics Journal 23(1), 1992
case_studies.what_it_is: The standard peer-reviewed debunking of golden-ratio claims about art, architecture, the body and aesthetics. It keeps phi's mathematical properties and rejects most of the empirical claims.
case_studies.how_it_works: It sets explicit measurement rules. Unstated measurements are assumed accurate to about 1%, and a 1% error in two lengths gives about 2% error in their ratio. That yields an 'acceptance range' of 1.58-1.66 for any claim of phi, and passing it is necessary but not sufficient. It notes that spirals of rectangles can be built from any ratio other than 1:1 (a sqrt(2) example) and cites Thompson for that. On Fechner, it quotes Zusne: 76% of choices fell on three rectangles (0.57, 0.62, 0.67), and many other rectangles were also chosen. In Markowsky's informal tests the most-chosen rectangle was 1.83, people could not find the golden rectangle among 48, and they could not see differences among rectangles between 1.6 and 1.7. It debunks the Parthenon, Pyramid, body and navel claims, and the 'golden' structure of the Aeneid, partly as artefacts of choosing which points to measure.
case_studies.relevance: It sets the honest contract for an engine that 'enforces' phi. Exactness is visually indistinguishable within a few percent, so phi earns its place as a coordinating constant shared across many elements, not as a perceptual magic number.
borrowable_ideas: Engine tolerance constant: treat a measured ratio within +/-2% of the target as 'golden' when fitting traced art. Report deviations in percent and pixels, not as pass/fail at five decimals.
Golden-ness checks should compare many elements to each other (do all leaves share one growth factor?), not each to 1.618 in isolation.

Let any rectangle ratio drive the 'whirling' construction (sqrt(2) is self-similar under halving). Do not hard-code phi into the construction primitive. Make the ratio a parameter whose default is phi.
case_studies.evidence: The WebFetch copies on cuhk and goldennumber.net were unreadable (one behind a captcha, one an image scan). Downloaded a JSTOR-scan PDF copy hosted at speakcdn and extracted text with pdftotext. Read the sections on spirals of rectangles, measurement tolerance and acceptance range, the Parthenon, the golden-rectangle aesthetics and Fechner section with Markowsky's experiments, and the human-body section.

case_studies.name: John Sharp, 'Spirals and the Golden Section', Nexus Network Journal 4(1), 2002
case_studies.what_it_is: A measured treatment of which spirals are actually 'golden', with measurements of nautilus shells.
case_studies.how_it_works: All the spirals discussed are logarithmic (equiangular), differing only in tangent angle and multiplication factor per turn. Sharp tabulates golden-section spirals from different gnomons. Rectangle: tangent angle 72.97 deg, factor phi^4 = 6.854 per turn (phi per 90 deg). LLS triangle: 75.68 deg, phi^(10/3) = 4.973 (phi per 108 deg). SSL triangle: 79.16 deg, phi^(5/2) = 3.330 (phi per 144 deg). Pentagon: 62.95 deg, phi^(20/3) = 24.73 (phi per 54 deg). His own nautilus measurements over 360 deg were 2.95, 3.02, 2.83 and 2.97 (mean 2.94; tangent about 80 deg). That is not the rectangle golden spiral. Closeness to the SSL spiral is called 'merely a coincidence'. A small change in tangent angle gives a large change in growth factor. The myth comes from a non-sequitur: shells are log spirals, phi can make a log spiral, so the nautilus must be golden.
case_studies.relevance: It gives the owner a legitimate menu of 'golden' growth rates, because the strict quarter-turn golden spiral is very open (6.85x per turn). It also kills the nautilus justification.
borrowable_ideas: Growth rule as 'phi per Theta', with Theta chosen from {54, 90, 108, 144, 180, 360} degrees. All of these are phi-derived, and Theta sets how tight the curl is. Derived figures: to grow 9x (Goldmann's volute span) takes 1.14 turns at phi per 90 deg, 1.83 turns at phi per 144 deg, and 2.28 turns at phi per 180 deg.

Show the tangent (pitch) angle as a designer-facing number alongside the growth factor. Small changes in angle cause big changes in growth, so a slider in angle space gives finer control near tight curls.
Don't call a nautilus-like spiral (about 3x per turn, roughly phi per 158 deg) golden in documentation.
case_studies.evidence: Opened the HTML article and read the measurement section, the golden-section spiral table, and the discussion of why the error persists. A Falbo 1.24-1.43 figure appeared only in a search snippet and was not verified.

case_studies.name: Ronald Hübner, 'Golden spiral or Fibonacci spiral: Which is more beautiful and why?' (2024)
case_studies.what_it_is: An online forced-choice experiment (N = 106) comparing a true golden logarithmic spiral with its quarter-circle Fibonacci approximation, and an Archimedean spiral with Dürer's half-circle approximation.
case_studies.how_it_works: Stimuli: a golden spiral (3.038 turns) versus a Fibonacci spiral of 11 quarter circles in Fibonacci squares (2.75 turns), and an Archimedean spiral (5 turns) versus a Dürer spiral of 10 half circles. Results: 79.2% preferred the golden spiral and 81.1% preferred the Archimedean. The parallel result supports the explanation: the originals have continuously changing curvature, while the approximations have constant curvature per arc with jumps at the joints. The author notes the differences are 'hardly visible', yet the preference is strong. He also says the Fibonacci spiral's beauty reputation rides on the phi 'beauty myth'. Limitations: only curvature continuity was tested, and originals were only compared with their own approximations.
case_studies.relevance: This is direct evidence that the engine's 'printed' quality depends on curvature-continuous primitives. The common designer shortcut, an Illustrator 'golden spiral' made of quarter circles, is measurably less preferred.
borrowable_ideas: Never ship quarter-circle (Fibonacci or compass) chains as final geometry. Use them only as construction guides. Render true log spirals approximated by cubic Beziers.

Rendering rule from my own numeric check (Python, Hermite cubic per segment on a golden spiral): max deviation is about 1.2% of local radius at 90 deg per segment, 0.24% at 60 deg, 0.076% at 45 deg and 0.015% at 30 deg. Use 45 deg or less for screen work and 30 deg or less for print or zoom.
Treat curvature continuity (G2) as a first-class validation check on every junction in the scene graph.
case_studies.evidence: Opened the PMC full text (methods, results, discussion and limitations), and the Wikipedia Golden spiral page that summarises it. A 2025 follow-up in Scientific Reports on individual spiral preferences could not be opened (Nature login redirect, PMC captcha).

case_studies.name: Renaissance compass volutes: Serlio, Salviati, Philandrier/Dürer (Andrey & Galli 2004), Goldmann's volute (Vollrath), and a programmatic re-implementation (Menezes Leitão)
case_studies.what_it_is: The classical straightedge-and-compass constructions for the Ionic volute, which reconstruct a vague passage in Vitruvius. Also a modern recursive code version of the same idea.
case_studies.how_it_works: Andrey & Galli redrew Serlio, Salviati and Philandrier, then plotted the radius increments. Serlio's and Salviati's volutes are three truncated Archimedean spirals: the radius decrement is constant within each turn and changes between turns. Salviati diminishes by 1/2 unit per quarter turn in the first turn, 1/3 in the second and 1/6 in the third, and he remarked on the curvature discontinuities at the transitions. Philandrier adopted Dürer's point-by-point spiral, which they identify as points on a tangent-function curve joined by arcs. They conclude the methods were not attempts to approximate any known curve such as a log or golden spiral. Goldmann (Vollrath, JOS): eye radius r, 12 quarter circles centred on the corners of three nested squares (sides r/3, 2r/3, r). The first radius is 7/6 r and the last 51/6 r, with the outer point 9r from the eye centre. Radii grow by the distance between successive centres, giving an involute of nested squares, which is piecewise arithmetic. Leitão's Julia/Khepri book recasts a volute as 'an arc followed by a smaller spiral'. spiral(p, r, a, da, fa, f) draws an arc, then recurses with the centre moved by r(1-f) along the end direction and radius r*f, so arc endpoints stay G1. da = pi, pi/2 or pi/4 imitates Serlio, Salviati or Philandrier.
case_studies.relevance: Victorian engravers inherited these compass methods, not phi. Their logic of a polygon of centres, radii and arcs is a good mental model for designers, and a geometric reduction factor f per arc makes them approximate a log spiral. The curvature jumps are the weakness that Hübner's study measures.
borrowable_ideas: A 'compass spiral' construction primitive (arc centres on a polygon path, radius increment equal to the side length) used as a guide layer that designers recognise from architecture drawing. The engine then fits a G2 log spiral or log-aesthetic curve through the arc endpoints for the final stroke.

Leitão's recursive signature (start point, radius, start angle, step angle, stop angle, reduction factor f) maps directly to a log spiral with f = e^(-b*da). For golden, f = 1/phi when da = 90 deg. Expose these exact parameters.
Use the volute's double line (fillet or listel) as the model for bundles that converge into an eye: a second, phase-shifted spiral, not a constant offset.
case_studies.evidence: Downloaded the Andrey & Galli Nexus 6(2) PDF and read its Salviati section, its Graph 1/2 analysis and its conclusions. The Vollrath PDF was saved by WebFetch and text-extracted; read the 'Goldmann's construction of a volute' section. Opened the Leitão Julia book page on the Ionic Order.

case_studies.name: Vogel's sunflower model, the golden angle, the three-gap theorem and golden-ratio low-discrepancy sequences
case_studies.what_it_is: Geometric models for spreading many elements evenly. Vogel (1979): r_n = c*sqrt(n), theta_n = n*137.508 deg. The 1D form is the additive recurrence x_n = frac(x0 + n/phi).
case_studies.how_it_works: Vogel's points lie on a Fermat spiral, and r proportional to sqrt(n) gives equal area per element. The golden angle is 360(1 - 1/phi) = 137.5078 deg = 2pi/phi^2. The pattern is described as highly sensitive to the angle, and ThatsMaths says one degree off 'breaks' it. Three-gap theorem: points at multiples of any angle around a circle have at most three distinct gaps, the largest being the sum of the other two. Phi's special status comes from being badly approximable, which gives the most uniform spacing (a Delone set), not fewer gap sizes. The golden-ratio additive recurrence has the lowest discrepancy of its kind. Thompson and ThatsMaths both stress the model is descriptive, not a biological explanation.
case_studies.relevance: This is the honest, mathematically grounded use of phi for 'clustered elements with a logical spread': stippling, beads, a rosette of many petals or dots, and choosing phases so repeated motifs never line up.
borrowable_ideas: A Vogel scatter operator for rosettes and medallion fills. Use the full-precision golden angle, because rounding errors accumulate as n times the error.
A 1D golden sequence for 'irregular but even' placement along a curve (beads, dots, small leaves): t_n = frac(t0 + 0.6180339887*n) in arc-length parameter, sorted.
Don't use golden-angle placement for small counts in a bilaterally symmetric frame. With few items the three-gap structure shows as visibly unequal gaps; use exact symmetric subdivision there.
case_studies.evidence: Opened MathWorld (Vogel spiral), Wikipedia Golden angle, Wikipedia Three-gap theorem, Wikipedia Low-discrepancy sequence, and the ThatsMaths sunflower article. Vogel's original paper (Math. Biosci. 44:179-189, doi 10.1016/0025-5564(79)90080-4) is paywalled and was not opened. Martin Roberts' quasirandom article returned 404 or gzip errors and was not used.

case_studies.name: Log-aesthetic curves (Harada; Miura; Yoshida & Saito), with the interactive G1/G2 Hermite method of Nagy, Yoshida & Hoffmann (2021)
case_studies.what_it_is: A one-parameter family of 'aesthetic' curves from Japanese industrial and automotive design. The log of radius of curvature against the log of arc-length increments (the logarithmic curvature graph, LCG) is a straight line with slope alpha.
case_studies.how_it_works: Fundamental equation: log(rho * ds/drho) = alpha*log(rho) + c. Yoshida et al. give closed-form relations for radius of curvature against tangent angle and arc length: rho(s) = e^(Lambda*s) for alpha = 0, and rho(s) = (Lambda*alpha*s + 1)^(1/alpha) otherwise. Points come from integrating exp(i*theta(s)). Special cases: alpha = -1 is the clothoid (Euler spiral), alpha = 1 the logarithmic spiral, alpha = 2 the circle involute, and alpha = 0 Nielsen's spiral. The original Yoshida method takes two endpoints, tangents and alpha, but only produces monotone-curvature segments. Nagy et al. extend it to segments that can have an inflection or curvature extremum. The segment is defined by endpoints, a tangent vector at the first point and a tangent direction at the second. Alpha is derived from the length of the first tangent vector, which controls start curvature and allows G2 joins between segments. Known restrictions: some boundary conditions have no solution for a given alpha, and evaluation needs numerical integration. Levien's thesis names log-aesthetic curves as possibly better than Euler spirals for some applications.
case_studies.relevance: This unifies the owner's two curve wishes, 'sweeps' and 'curls', in one primitive. A golden curl is the alpha = 1 member, the easement into it is near alpha = -1, and alpha becomes a character dial for leaves and flames. Harada's reported link between LCG slope and impression (centripetal or sharp versus accelerating) gives designers a vocabulary.
borrowable_ideas: One 'aesthetic segment' primitive with parameters (P0, T0, P1, T1, alpha). Golden curls are alpha = 1 with the extra constraint b = 0.30635, so rho = b*s measured from the pole (my derivation from the log-spiral arc-length and curvature formulas on Wikipedia).
Expose alpha as a 'character' slider for leaf blades and flame tongues, and keep alpha = 1 plus golden b for curls.
G2 chaining: segments share endpoint curvature, so a leaf blade flows into its curl without a visible kink.
case_studies.evidence: WebFetch saved the arXiv PDF and I extracted it with pdftotext. Read the abstract, the introduction (Harada, Miura and LCG definitions; Levien's remark) and Section 2 equations (2)-(6). Special-case slopes come from search snippets of Yoshida's notebook and an arXiv polar-LAC paper; the slope sign convention varies between papers.

case_studies.name: Raph Levien: the Euler spiral history, 'From Spiral to Spline' (Spiro), and Euler-spiral parallel curves
case_studies.what_it_is: A PhD thesis and open-source Spiro spline library (used in FontForge and as an Inkscape pen and path-effect mode). The designer places points on the curve and the engine computes a fair G2 or G4 curve built from Euler-spiral segments. A companion tech report covers the Euler spiral's history as the railway transition curve.
case_studies.how_it_works: The Euler spiral has curvature linear in arc length. It was posed by Bernoulli, solved by Euler, and reinvented by Fresnel and by Talbot, whose 1890 railway transition spiral has 'degree-of-curve increasing directly as the distance'. The thesis shows that an extensional interpolating spline (adding an on-curve point doesn't change the shape) whose segments form a two-parameter family must cut every segment from one generating curve. The Euler spiral is a strong all-round choice, and it converts to cubic Beziers at interactive speed. Spiro point types (FontForge docs): G4 curve, G2 curve, corner, and left/right constraint points for line-to-curve transitions. Caveat: moving a point too far can make the solver fail into 'erratic spirals'. On parallel curves, a cusp appears where the offset equals the source's radius of curvature. Euler-spiral pieces have closed-form offset curvature, so cusps can be located and split before fitting.
case_studies.relevance: This is the best precedent for making mathematically fair curves designable by someone used to Illustrator: on-curve points plus typed constraints instead of Bezier handles. The railway transition is the right model for where the straight side ribbons enter the corner scrolls.
borrowable_ideas: Ribbon-to-curl 'easement': join a straight band (kappa = 0) to a golden curl of entry curvature kappa0 with an Euler-spiral segment whose curvature ramps linearly from 0 to kappa0, as in a railway transition spiral.

Author the dominant curves as Spiro-like on-curve points with typed nodes (G2 curve, corner, line-to-curve constraint). Then add special nodes such as 'golden-curl start' that lock the remainder of the curve to an exact golden spiral.

Offset rule for clustered lines: an inner parallel at distance d cusps where rho = d. On a golden spiral rho = b*s from the pole, so an inside offset must end before arc length s = d/b, about 3.26d from the pole (where local r is about 0.956d). After that, switch to a phase-rotated spiral.
case_studies.evidence: Opened the EECS-2009-162 abstract page. Downloaded and text-extracted the EECS-2008-111 Euler-spiral history PDF and read the abstract and the Talbot and spline sections. Opened the FontForge Spiro editing page and Levien's raphlinus.github.io parallel-curves post. Inkscape Spiro mode details come from search snippets of Inkscape forum and mailing-list posts.

case_studies.name: B. de Smit & H. W. Lenstra Jr., 'The Mathematical Structure of Escher's Print Gallery' (Notices AMS, 2003)
case_studies.what_it_is: An analysis of how Escher's self-similar, spiralling lithograph can be produced by complex logarithm and exponential maps, and a reconstruction of the conformal grid Escher was trying to draw.
case_studies.how_it_works: A picture invariant under scaling (a 'cyclic expansion' by 256x per cycle in Escher's straight study) becomes periodic when pulled back by the exponential map. A conformal map h(w) = w^gamma = exp(gamma*log w) turns the straight version into the curved one. The resulting image contains a copy of itself rotated by 157.6 deg and scaled down by 22.58x. Conformality means small squares stay square, so local motifs are only rotated and scaled, never sheared.
case_studies.relevance: It shows how to make 'everything relative to a dominant spiral' authorable. The designer draws a straight strip of repeated motifs, and the engine wraps it into a golden scroll. Every motif becomes an exactly similar, geometrically diminishing copy, the gnomon property, automatically.
borrowable_ideas: A 'spiral strip' layout. Author in w-space, a flat band with motifs repeated at a fixed spacing along the direction (b + i). Map with z = O + exp(w). Straight lines along that direction become golden spirals (exp(ln a + (b+i)t) = a*e^{bt}*e^{it}), and translation by (b+i)*delta becomes the spiral similarity z -> e^{(b+i)delta}*z.
Because the map is conformal, leaf angles and tangent junctions drawn in the flat strip are preserved in the scroll, which preserves Owen-Jones-style tangential junctions.
Keep motifs small relative to the local radius and stop before the pole, which is a singularity. Larger motifs show a natural-looking taper (the far side grows faster).
case_studies.evidence: Downloaded the 6-page PDF and text-extracted it. Read the passages on cyclic expansion, the exponential map and period lattice, the conformal grid, and the 157.6 deg / 22.58x result.

case_studies.name: Victorian design grammar: Owen Jones, The Grammar of Ornament (1856), Propositions 8-13, and Christopher Dresser, Principles of Decorative Design (1873)
case_studies.what_it_is: Rules for ornament written by the period designers whose aesthetic the site imitates.
case_studies.how_it_works: Jones, as summarised on readingdesign.org: Prop 8, ornament on a geometric construction. Prop 9, definite proportions on a simple unit, with subtle ratios such as 5:8 preferred to 4:8. Prop 10, balance of straight, inclined and curved lines. Prop 11, every line grows from a parent stem, and every ornament however distant can be traced to its branch and root. Prop 12, junctions of curves with curves or straights should be tangential. Prop 13, conventionalise natural forms rather than copying them. Dresser (primary text): curves are beautiful in proportion to their subtlety, and the arc is the least beautiful because its single centre is instantly detected. Ellipse and egg curves drawn with string or trammel beat compass arcs. Proportion should be subtle: 1:1 and 2:1 are bad, while 3:8, 5:8 and 5:13 are good, because pleasure grows with the difficulty of detecting the ratio. Order and orderly repetition are principles of ornament. He also praises the nautilus for 'following... a particular geometrical curve with rigid precision', which is the Victorian intuition behind the owner's request.
case_studies.relevance: The owner's 'dominant functions with dependent elements' is Jones's Prop 11, and 'leaf integrated into the sweep' is Prop 12. Dresser's arc critique anticipates Hübner's curvature result. Dresser also frames Fibonacci ratios as subtle rather than mystical, which is the honest framing.
borrowable_ideas: Scene-graph rule: every element must declare a parent curve and an attachment parameter (t or arc length). Orphan strokes fail validation (Prop 11).
Junction validator: G1 is required (Prop 12) and G2 is preferred (Hübner, Dresser).
Proportion palette for crest and cartouche subdivisions from Fibonacci fractions (3:5, 5:8, 8:13, 5:13). These sit within Markowsky's tolerance of phi but read as deliberate integers.
No compass-arc primitives in final output. Arcs are construction-only, in line with Dresser's ranking.
case_studies.evidence: Downloaded the Dresser Gutenberg text (#39749) and read the 'Curves will be found to be beautiful...' and 'Proportion... subtle' passages and the nautilus passage. Owen Jones propositions come from the readingdesign.org page via WebFetch summary. I did not read a primary scan of Jones, though a Wisconsin digital-copy snippet confirms the 'parent stem' and 'tangential curvature' wording.

case_studies.name: Proportional scales as designer tools: Tim Brown's modular scale (A List Apart, 2011) and Le Corbusier's Modulor
case_studies.what_it_is: Two precedents for giving designers a discrete palette of phi-derived values instead of asking them to compute ratios.
case_studies.how_it_works: Modular scale: choose a ratio (for example phi) and a base, then multiply and divide to get a sequence (10 gives 16.18, 26.18, 6.18, 3.82). A double-stranded scale interleaves two bases or ratios to fill gaps. Designers pick values from the scale for sizes, measures and margins, round them, combine them, or break from the scale, recording the derivation with 'comment math'. Brown calls scales 'a tool, not magic'. Modulor: red and blue series built by golden division from navel height (1.13 m) and raised-arm height (2.26 m) of a 1.83 m man, rounded to round numbers. It governed the dimensions of the Unité d'Habitation and La Tourette. Its human basis was revised for cultural rather than measured reasons.
case_studies.relevance: This is the realistic workflow answer to 'how do I design inside phi constraints'. Offer a palette of snapped values and log the deviations, rather than demanding the designer compute.
borrowable_ideas: Design tokens: a phi-scale of stroke gaps, leaf sizes and band widths (base times phi^(k/n), with n = 1, 2 or 3 for finer steps) exported to Illustrator as a swatch-like reference sheet and to the engine as named constants.
'Comment math' in the engine: any hand-entered value that is off-scale must carry a reason string. The deviation report shows it.
Double-stranded scales (phi steps from two bases) give enough choices to avoid the designer fighting the system.
case_studies.evidence: Opened the A List Apart article and the Wikipedia Modulor page.

case_studies.name: Harriss spiral (Edmund Harriss; Chalkdust magazine)
case_studies.what_it_is: A branching analogue of the golden-rectangle spiral. A rectangle in the plastic ratio (about 1.3247, root of x^3 = x + 1) splits into one square and two similar rectangles, and arcs drawn in the squares line up into a tree of spirals.
case_studies.how_it_works: The golden rectangle splits into a square plus one similar rectangle, giving a single spiral chain. The plastic rectangle splits into a square plus two similar rectangles, so recursion branches. Two arcs are drawn per square and chosen to meet the arcs in the sub-rectangles. The page does not give the exact radii or centres.
case_studies.relevance: Acanthus scrolls branch: side scrolls spring from the main stem. This is the cleanest known self-similar branching-spiral construction. It is not golden, which matters if the owner wants strict phi.
borrowable_ideas: A recursive 'rectangle-split' layout generator (ratio as a parameter) to place where secondary scrolls branch off a dominant scroll, each branch a similar copy.
Use it as a guide layer, then refit the arcs as G2 curves (same curvature-jump caveat as Fibonacci arcs).
case_studies.evidence: Opened the Chalkdust 'On the cover: Harriss spiral' page. Background on Harriss and a 2023 Bridges integer variant came from search snippets only.

principles.principle: Construction (a): to make the curve through a set of leaf tips a golden spiral, generate the leaves by one repeated spiral similarity about a pole. Do not place the tips by hand.
principles.source: Thompson, On Growth and Form (gnomon propositions); Wikipedia Spiral similarity (complex form T(x) = x0 + alpha(x - x0)); Golden spiral page (b = ln(phi)/(pi/2))
principles.apply_how: In complex coordinates choose the pole O, master leaf L0 (with anchors base0 and tip0), angular step dTheta (for example 45 deg) and growth rule 'phi per Theta' (Theta = 90 deg for strict golden). Set c = phi^(dTheta/Theta) * e^(+/- i*dTheta) and L_k = O + c^k (L0 - O). At 45 deg the leaf sizes go 1, 1.272, 1.618, 2.058, 2.618. If the designer instead draws two leaves, compute the transform from corresponding anchors: alpha = (tip1 - base1)/(tip0 - base0) and O = (base0*tip1 - tip0*base1)/(base0 + tip1 - tip0 - base1). Then snap |alpha| to phi^(arg(alpha)/Theta). For traced art with named tip anchors, fit a log spiral: for a candidate O, regress ln|z_k - O| on unwrapped angle theta_k, and minimise the residual over O (2D search). Report b against 0.30635 and per-tip residuals in px, and offer 'snap' (keep O and the fitted angles, set b to golden).

principles.principle: Construction (b): make each leaf's curl an exact golden spiral that joins its incoming stroke with matching tangent and curvature (G2), so it reads as one sweep.
principles.source: Logarithmic spiral formulas (Wikipedia: kappa = 1/(r*sqrt(1+k^2)), arc length (r2 - r1)/sin(alpha)); Levien (Euler-spiral easement, G2 Spiro points); Hübner (curvature continuity)
principles.apply_how: Inputs: entry point P, forward tangent T (direction toward the eye), and entry curvature kappa0, taken from the incoming blade or stem curve. With golden b = 0.30635, the pole lies 72.97 deg off the forward tangent, on the inside of the turn, at distance r0 = cos(17.03 deg)/kappa0 = 0.9562/kappa0. The radius then shrinks by exactly phi every quarter turn. Stop at eye radius r_e after ln(r0/r_e)/b radians. Total length from entry to the pole is rho0/b, about 3.26 times the entry radius of curvature. If the incoming stroke is straight, insert an Euler-spiral easement whose curvature ramps 0 to kappa0. Use the same b and the same r_e/r0 on every curl so all curls are similar copies.

principles.principle: Construction (c): spread clustered lines by one of four rules chosen by context, never by eye.
principles.source: Andrey & Galli (volute fillets), Levien (offset cusps), Markowsky and Dresser (subtle ratios), Vogel and golden-angle sources, Wikipedia low-discrepancy sequence
principles.apply_how: (1) Near a spiral eye, use phase-rotated copies of the dominant spiral: line_j = O + e^{-(b+i)*j*delta}(S - O). Gaps then stay a constant fraction of radius and converge into the eye with no cusps. Pick delta = -ln(1 - g/R)/b for gap g at radius R. (2) Along ribbons and straight-ish sweeps, use true constant offsets (engraved hatching look). Stop each inside offset d where local radius of curvature reaches d. (3) For lines converging to an edge, use geometric gaps g_j = g0*q^j with q = phi^(-1/n), n in {1,2,3}. Total width is g0/(1-q), which is phi^2*g0 for q = 1/phi. Truncate when a gap would fall below the minimum printable gap. (4) For many-element organic clusters (stipple, rosettes), use Vogel r = c*sqrt(n), theta = n*137.50776 deg, or the 1D sequence frac(t0 + 0.618034n) along arc length. Use Fibonacci counts (3, 5, 8) for the number of lines per cluster.

principles.principle: Exact repetition under one transform plus curvature continuity is what reads as 'printed'. Phi exactness does not.
principles.source: Hübner 2024; Markowsky 1992; Dresser 1873
principles.apply_how: Treat G2 junctions and shared growth factors as hard engine constraints. Treat the specific value phi as a default parameter checked within +/-2%. Ship true log spirals and Euler or log-aesthetic segments, approximated by cubic Beziers of 45 deg or less (30 deg or less for print); Fibonacci or compass arc chains are guides only.

principles.principle: Every element is a child of a dominant curve and joins it tangentially.
principles.source: Owen Jones, Grammar of Ornament, Props 11-12; Spiro constraint points (Levien/FontForge)
principles.apply_how: Scene graph: each node stores (parent curve id, attachment arc-length or t, local frame from the parent's tangent and normal, continuity requirement). Validation fails for orphans or G0-only joins. Moving a dominant curve re-evaluates all dependents, which is how the frame adapts to page size.

principles.principle: 'Golden' is a family of growth rates. Pick the tightness, keep the derivation.
principles.source: Sharp 2002 (rectangle, LLS, SSL and pentagon golden spirals)
principles.apply_how: Growth parameter 'phi per Theta' with Theta in {54, 90, 108, 144, 180, 360} degrees: 24.7x, 6.85x, 4.97x, 3.33x, 2.62x and 1.62x per turn. Use 90 deg for open sweeps such as the flame envelope, and 144-180 deg for multi-turn curls and volutes. A classical volute's 9x over 3 turns averages about phi per 236 deg, which is my derived figure.

principles.principle: Author flat, wrap conformally.
principles.source: de Smit & Lenstra 2003; Thompson Ch. XVII (coordinate transformations)
principles.apply_how: Let the designer draw a straight repeating strip of leaves in a unit grid, then map it with z = O + exp(w) along direction (b+i) to get a golden scroll. Conformality preserves the drawn angles and tangent junctions, and every repeat becomes an exact similar copy.

principles.principle: Use phi as a coordinating palette with logged deviations, not as a mandate.
principles.source: Tim Brown modular scale; Modulor; Cook's deviation thesis
principles.apply_how: Expose design tokens on a phi-scale (base*phi^(k/n)). Allow off-scale values only with a recorded reason, and generate a deviation report per artwork (element, target, actual, percent, px).

principles.principle: Give the curve a 'character' parameter rather than many handles.
principles.source: Log-aesthetic curves (Harada; Miura; Yoshida & Saito; Nagy et al. 2021)
principles.apply_how: A segment primitive (P0, T0, P1, T1, alpha): alpha = 1 for golden curls (with b locked), around -1 for easements and sweeps, and tuned for leaf blades and flame tongues. Join segments with G2 by matching endpoint curvature.

cautions: Nautilus shells are log spirals but not golden ones. Sharp measured about 2.94x per turn against 6.85x for the golden spiral. Don't justify the engine with nature claims; justify it with self-similarity and consistency.

Classical Ionic volutes (Serlio, Salviati, Goldmann) are compass-built, piecewise-Archimedean arc chains with acknowledged curvature jumps, not golden spirals (Andrey & Galli). 'The volute is golden' is a myth. Victorian engravers used compass and machine constructions, not phi.

Phi precision is perceptually invisible within a few percent. Markowsky: people can't tell rectangles between 1.6 and 1.7 apart. McManus et al. 2010 (from secondary summaries): group preference for the golden rectangle is weak, while individual preferences are strong and highly variable. Don't promise viewers will 'feel' phi.

The strict quarter-turn golden spiral is very open (6.85x per turn). Getting 9x radius change takes only about 1.14 turns, so forcing it onto a multi-turn curl gives a tiny eye or a huge outer whorl. Use a slower phi-derived growth (phi per 144-180 deg) or accept a non-golden b.

Quarter-circle 'golden spiral' templates, including Illustrator overlays, are Fibonacci spirals. Their curvature jumps by a factor of phi at every joint, and Hübner found them less preferred (about 21% vs 79%). Never let them leak into final geometry.
Thompson: log spirals belong to accretive growth. Forcing whole leaf outlines or blade margins onto spirals will look mechanical in the wrong way. Constrain tips, stems and curls, not every contour.

Inner offsets of a spiral cusp where the offset distance equals the local radius of curvature (on a golden spiral, once local r is below about 0.96 times the offset). Bundles must switch to phase-rotated spirals or terminate before the eye.

Phi-geometric spacing decays fast. With q = 1/phi the 6th gap is 9% of the first, which collides with hairline widths and causes moire or aliasing on screen. Use phi^(-1/2) or phi^(-1/3) steps, cap line counts, and enforce a minimum device-pixel gap that is recomputed on resize.

Golden-angle and Vogel placement is very sensitive to the angle (one degree off breaks the pattern), and it looks irregular with small counts (three-gap theorem). It suits stipple and rosettes, not a symmetric banknote-style frame that needs mirror symmetry.

Over-constraining kills designability. Spiro solvers can blow up into 'erratic spirals' when points move far, and log-aesthetic Hermite problems have no solution for some boundary conditions and need numerical integration. The engine needs graceful fallbacks, clamping and undo, plus explicit override slots (Cook, Brown).
Conformal exp wrapping has a singular pole and scales motifs non-uniformly across their extent. Keep motifs small relative to local radius and stop before the eye.
The Harriss branching spiral uses the plastic ratio (about 1.3247), not phi. If the owner insists on 'everything golden', a branching scroll construction will need a different rule.

Some sources were only partially verified: Vogel's original paper is paywalled; Owen Jones' propositions come from a secondary summary; log-aesthetic special-case slope conventions differ between papers; and a 2025 Scientific Reports follow-up on spiral preference could not be opened.

angles.summary: Professional engraved and security-printed line work does not look "printed" because of texture. It looks printed because every line belongs to a family generated from a few guide curves, and line weight is a continuous function, not a fixed stroke width. Ostromoukhov's Digital Facial Engraving shows the core model. A designer draws four border curves in Illustrator, the engine re-parametrizes them by arc length, builds a Coons-patch grid, and turns iso-parametric lines into engraved lines by thresholding a sawtooth "universal copperplate". Lines therefore swell and taper to nothing on their own, and layers merge by min/max rules to make cross-hatching. DigiDürer gives a second model that maps closely to "dominant functions": each line is a propagated front (equipotential) of an initial curve, with spacing set by a speed field. It also names the three properties that make classical line work read well: lines never cross, run roughly parallel and stay smooth. Real rose-engine guilloché supplies the answer for "logical spread". One waveform is repeated N times, and only a fixed step and a deterministic phase sequence change between cuts: constant, half-pitch for barleycorn, a linear ramp, a zigzag, or even Fibonacci for the "sinewave" moiré. Guilloche software makes the same idea explicit with envelopes: a sinusoid is mapped between an inner and an outer envelope curve. Commercial security tools (Agfa Arziro as an Illustrator plug-in, Jura Corvina Engraver) confirm the workflow is hybrid. Designers draw guide paths and freehand key strokes, and generators fill in the line families. In the browser, the realistic split is crisp vector geometry, with variable width baked into filled outline polygons because SVG has no variable-width stroke. A separate, static "ink" layer can add ink gain (blur plus threshold, or dilate) and very low-amplitude displacement. WebGL threshold shading is the option for very dense fills. Animated or large-area feTurbulence/feDisplacementMap is a known performance and crash risk, and noise quickly reads as grunge rather than engraving.

case_studies.name: Digital Facial Engraving (Victor Ostromoukhov, SIGGRAPH 99)
case_studies.what_it_is: A system that imitates copperplate engraving. Engraving layers are built over an image and merged with masks, and the paper is the base reference for digital engraving in security and stamp printing.
case_studies.how_it_works: (1) Basic engraving layer: uniformly spaced waves on a unit square in (u,v) space, each with a sawtooth cross-section modelled on the triangular furrow a burin cuts. This is a 'universal copperplate' threshold structure. Comparing the input tone to it gives a line whose width is proportional to darkness, so engraving equals ordered dithering with a designed threshold matrix. (2) Warping: each layer is mapped into the image by a Coons patch P(u,v)=(1-v)U1(u)+vU2(u)+(1-u)L(v)+uR(v), where L(v)=V1(v)-(1-v)V1(0)-vV1(1) and R(v) is defined the same way. The four border curves are straight lines or Bézier segments 'easily created... using Adobe Illustrator'. Each border curve is re-parametrized for uniform arc length, so curves with different segment counts and lengths interpolate smoothly. (3) Merging: each layer gets a range scale S and range shift D (T' = T*S + D), painted as masks. Merge modes are copy, smaller (MIN, which produces cross-etching), bigger (MAX, continuous lines in darks), multiply and add. Abrupt mask edges give clean junctions between layers; soft edges give gradual overlap. (4) Equilibration: the threshold matrix is corrected locally and iteratively with a dot-gain and human-visual-system model, so uniform input always gives uniform perceived tone. It is computed at 16 levels and interpolated. When an accent layer of strokes parallel to a feature was added, equilibration automatically thinned the surrounding lines. (5) An 'engraving style' is a reusable set of layers plus masks that carries over to new images. Deliberate irregular perturbation, mezzotint layers, and abrupt changes of direction or frequency are used as expressive contrast tools.
case_studies.relevance: This is the closest published model of what the user describes. A few designer-drawn 'dominant' curves define a patch, and every engraved line is an iso-curve of that patch, so all lines are positioned relative to the guide curves. Line weight comes from a function, so lines swell and taper with mechanical consistency instead of hand-drawn variation.
borrowable_ideas: Patch primitive: four named Illustrator paths (top, bottom, left, right) become a Coons patch. Line families are iso-u or iso-v curves at a chosen pitch, so the medallion's leaf hatching follows the sweep of the stem.
Re-parametrize every imported guide curve by arc length with a lookup table before use, so u=0.5 always means halfway along the curve whatever its Bézier segment count.
Width as a threshold: width(u,v) = pitch * clamp(tone(u,v)) for each line. Lines taper to zero wherever tone reaches zero, so tapering comes from the tone field and not from line caps.
Merge modes as engine operations: MIN for cross-hatching that breaks up in highlights, MAX for lines that stay continuous in darks, and copy with a mask for clean hand-offs between line families.
Accent strokes with equilibration: adding a contour-hugging accent line thins its neighbours so the local tone stays constant.
Reusable 'style' objects (pitch, angle, merge mode, width curve) that a designer applies to any new patch.
case_studies.evidence: Downloaded the full PDF and read all sections: Rationale, 2.1 Building layers with the Coons patch (eq. 1), 2.2 Superimposition with the Table 1 merge modes, 2.3 Equilibration, 3 B/W engraving, 3.3 Enhancements, 3.4 Engraving style, 4 Color, 5 Future work.

case_studies.name: Artistic Halftoning – Between Technology and Art (Ostromoukhov, SPIE 2000; covers Artistic Screening SIGGRAPH 95 and Multicolor/Artistic Dithering SIGGRAPH 99)
case_studies.what_it_is: An overview of halftoning methods whose screen elements are designed shapes (ornaments, letters, microtext), with applications to banknote and anti-counterfeiting design.
case_studies.how_it_works: A graphic designer draws dot contours in Adobe Illustrator at a few fixed intensity levels. All contours are cubic Béziers, and straight parts are also stored as Bézier control polygons, so every contour has a compatible structure. Shape blending then interpolates the contours for all 256 levels, and each level is rasterized in advance with non-zero winding. The definition space and the rendition space are separate, and the mapping between them can be non-linear. Examples are a conformal map w = k(1+z+e^z) that bends a rectangular grid of motifs along electromagnetic field lines, and w = tg(z), which produces a non-repeating microletter screen on an imaginary banknote that resists scanning without moiré. Multi-color dithering lays inks side by side without overlap. Partially random dither matrices keep motifs readable across a wider tone range.
case_studies.relevance: It shows a designer-friendly split. The designer draws a few keyframe shapes, the engine interpolates the in-between shapes and warps a regular arrangement of them along curved fields. Conformal (angle-preserving) maps keep each motif's proportions while the field bends, which is what leaves strung along a sweeping curve need.
borrowable_ideas: Keyframed motifs: the designer draws a leaf at 2-3 'growth' states with the same anchor count and order, and the engine blends between them by parameter (size, position along the spine).
Enforce compatible Bézier topology on import (same number of segments and the same start point) and flag violations to the designer, because interpolation fails otherwise.
Separate definition space from rendition space. Ornament rows are authored straight in a unit strip, then mapped onto a dominant curve with an angle-preserving warp so leaves are not sheared.
Microtext or motif screens as a fill style for bands such as the bead or lattice bands.
case_studies.evidence: Downloaded the PDF and read the abstract, §1, §2 Artistic screening (contour interpolation, conformal mappings, banknote microletters), §3 Multi-color dithering, §3.5 partially random matrices, and the start of §4.

case_studies.name: DigiDürer – a digital engraving system (Pnueli & Bruckstein, The Visual Computer 1994)
case_studies.what_it_is: An engraving and halftoning system in which every line is a level contour of a potential field grown outward from an initial curve.
case_studies.how_it_works: The authors note that lines in classic engravings are (1) non-intersecting, (2) approximately parallel and (3) smooth except at edges, which are the properties of equipotential lines. To keep tone correct, the local density of lines measured normal to the lines must be proportional to the grey level. They solve the Eikonal equation |∇H| = g(x,y), using an initial line L(s,0) as the boundary condition, and draw contours of H every ΔH, with ΔH proportional to line width w. In practice this is front propagation: each point of the current line moves a distance dt along its normal so that dH = g·dt, and the result is the next line. Known problems are fronts that fail to cover the whole picture (so propagation also runs in the reverse direction) and topological problems such as shocks and cusps. For each decision (for example the choice of initial curve) the system takes input from a built-in algorithm, the user, or externally supplied 'side information'.
case_studies.relevance: This is the formal version of 'dominant functions with lines relative to them'. The dominant curve is the initial front, and every sibling line is a propagated copy of it, spaced by a speed field. A speed field can encode any logical spread, including a phi progression, and the result stays parallel and never crosses.
borrowable_ideas: Offset-family generator: given a dominant curve and a spacing function d_k (constant, geometric by φ, Fibonacci, eased), produce lines as offsets or fronts at cumulative distances, with optional variation along the curve (g(s)).
Make 'non-intersecting, approximately parallel, smooth' a validator that rejects or trims any generated family that breaks it.
Detect shocks and cusps where fronts collide (high curvature on the concave side) and end lines there with a taper, the way engravers stop lines.
Three-source parameter design: every engine decision gets a computed default, a designer override in Illustrator, and a data-driven option.
case_studies.evidence: Downloaded the PDF and read the abstract, §1, §2 and §3.1–3.2 (the Eikonal formulation, the equipotential-contour algorithm, the list of classic line properties and the topological problems).

case_studies.name: Rose engine & straightline engine guilloché (G. Phil Poirier, SNAG Technical Article Part 2, 2016)
case_studies.what_it_is: A practitioner's technical account of how mechanical guilloché machines produce their patterns: rosettes, phasing, cutter geometry and rules for developing patterns.
case_studies.how_it_works: A rosette cam with N lobes rocks the headstock against a fixed touch while the cutter stays still. Cuts run from the outside toward the centre with a fixed radial step. Hundreds of patterns come from one rosette by changing only the phase between cuts. Zero phase gives a concentric pattern. A half-pitch shift gives barleycorn (a 24-lobe rosette turned 1/48 of a circle, 7.5°). A constant 1° per cut gives a pinwheel. ±1° for 5 cuts and then the reverse gives lightning or zigzag. Worm adjustments 'resemble the Fibonacci sequence, 1,2,3,5,8,13,8,5,3,2,1' to give the radiating sinewave or moiré pattern. Straightline engines work the same way: a half-pitch crossing-slide offset gives barleycorn, and a small increment per cut gives a diagonal. The touch radius relative to the lobe radius sets the waveform: exactly ½ gives a sine, less gives concave scallops, more gives convex scallops. Moving the touch to the other side mirrors the pattern. Amplitude stays constant while the radius shrinks, so the centre turns 'muddy' and guillochers cut plain circles there. The cutter has a 150–160° included angle, and depth controls width, so lines within a family have constant width.
case_studies.relevance: This is the historical, mechanical proof that 'clustered lines with logical spread' means one base waveform, N copies, a fixed step and a deterministic phase sequence. It also shows that Fibonacci-governed spacing is a real guilloché technique, not just a decorative idea, which ties directly to the user's golden-ratio goal.
borrowable_ideas: LineFamily = {baseWave(t), count N, stepFn(k), phaseFn(k), widthFn}. phaseFn presets: constant, alternating half-pitch (barleycorn), linear ramp (pinwheel), zigzag(n) (lightning), Fibonacci up and down (sinewave), and φ-geometric.
Waveform 'touch' parameter: one scalar morphs a lobe between concave scallop, sine and convex scallop, which gives designers one intuitive slider.
Mirror toggle (touch on the opposite side) for symmetric side ribbons.
Scale amplitude with local radius or curvature, and automatically switch to plain curves where spacing would collapse ('anti-mud' rule).
Constant line width within a family (fixed cutter depth); vary width between families to create hierarchy.
case_studies.evidence: Downloaded the PDF and extracted the text. Read Part II (machines, cutting tool), Part III (pattern development for rose and straightline engines, including the Fibonacci phase sequence) and the touch/rosette relationship section.

case_studies.name: Envelope-based guilloche rosettes and borders (Stephen M. Cameron, 'Playing Around With Guilloche Patterns' slides + Processing code) with the Variable Guilloche patent US8289579B2
case_studies.what_it_is: An open-source (MIT, Processing) step-by-step build of guilloche rosettes and frames, plus a patent that lists the polar curve families used in security guilloche.
case_studies.how_it_works: Spirograph wheels along a path give one family. True rosettes instead map a sinusoid between envelopes: r(t) = inner(t) + (outer(t) − inner(t))·(s(t)+0.5), where s is a sinusoid scaled to [−0.5, 0.5].
