findings.question: Q2a: main S-sweep #113 (stem at 72.85,321.82 -> around medallion -> 171.9,187.8) and parallel sweep #114: curvature model
findings.result:
#113 (length 765u) has inflections at s=34, 132.6 (109.6,234.7), 610.7 and 670.1.
- Upper limb (inflection at s=133 to peak |k| at s=265, 135u, 51 deg turn): curvature grows from 0 to 0.0139. Clothoid R2 0.980; power law k~s^1.10 R2 0.988; exponential R2 0.81; log spiral (Cesaro) R2 0.03. Golden-b spiral forced: RMS 1.31, max 3.16.
- Lower limb (back toward the stem, 76u): k~s^1.58 R2 0.93; clothoid R2 0.80; log spiral R2 0.05.
- #114 upper limb: clothoid R2 0.97, p=1.16. #114 lower limb: p=1.48, R2 0.95.
- Medallion arc segments 2-3 (s 290-560, 268u, 170 deg turn): near-circular, curvature 0.0066-0.0136, coefficient of variation 0.18. Circle fit r=85.76 centred at (129.89,134.14), RMS 0.54, max 2.19. That centre is 3.5u below the ellipse centre (129.82,130.63); distance from the ellipse centre ranges 82.4-88.0. Ratio r / mean ellipse radius (71.42) = 1.20.
- Bottom stem x positions: 32.94, 44.45, 61.34, 72.85. Gaps 11.51 / 16.89 / 11.51 (two 2-line ribbons); middle/outer gap = 1.467.
findings.phi_comparison: The S-limbs are clothoids (Euler spirals): curvature is close to linear in arc length (p about 1.1). The ring part is a circular arc. Neither is a log spiral. The 1.20 ring/ellipse ratio is not phi. The stem gap ratio of 1.467 is 9% under phi; if made golden, the middle gap would be 18.62 instead of 16.89 (+1.7u).

findings.question: Q2b: right-hand scroll curl #103 (and the top scroll end of #0): log-spiral fit
findings.result:
#103 inner curl (segments 4-10, 88u long, about 640 deg wound):
- Free log spiral: pole (241.91,111.34), |b|=0.16, growth 1.29 per quarter turn and 2.76 per full turn. RMS 1.43, max 10.2 (poor).
- Local b in a sliding +-90 deg window wanders 0.52 -> 0.13 -> 0.21 -> 0.01 -> 0.43, so the curl is not one spiral.
- Radius ratios between successive turns along rays from the pole: 1.95-5.0.
- Innermost 1.5 turns (segments 5-10): log spiral b=0.144 (2.47 per turn) RMS 0.41, versus Archimedean pitch 4.73u/turn RMS 0.39. The two fit equally well.
- Golden b forced: RMS 2.83, max 4.42.
- Including the outer loop (segments 3-10): free b=0.27, RMS 4.65 (fit fails).

#0 top-right scroll (last 3 segments, 115u): free b=0.36 (1.76 per quarter turn), RMS 3.53, max 6.8, local b 0.25-0.83. Golden forced: RMS 3.94 (no real difference, both poor).

The end loops of #0 and #61 are teardrop loops, not spirals (RMS 6-8).
findings.phi_comparison: The #103 curl is much tighter than golden: about 2.5-2.8 growth per turn against phi^4 = 6.85. Its b of 0.14-0.16 is about half of golden. Rebuilding it as golden at the same outer size would leave about half as many visible turns, or need a far smaller eye; this is a visible change. The #0 scroll averages b 0.36, near golden, but the fit is too poor to support the claim.

findings.question: Q2c: clustered nested lines: spacing and ratios of successive gaps
findings.result:
Family A, tendrils #28-#34 (7 lines):
- All end exactly at (57.04,130.62), the leftmost point of the medallion ellipse.
- Lines cross: the order goes 1,0,2,...
- Gaps at mid-length: 2.56/2.78/2.99/3.39/2.90/2.29 (coefficient of variation 0.12, successive ratios 0.79-1.14). At 40%: 1.43-5.05 (ratios 0.9-1.93). At 75%: 1.74 -> 0.69, decreasing (geometric 0.81).

Family B, #55-#60 (6 lines):
- All end exactly at (173.57,186.62), which lies on the ellipse.
- Open-end start spacing 2.37/2.65/2.38/2.58/2.55 (even, coefficient of variation about 5%).
- Mid gaps 0.69/1.00/0.68/0.92/0.68 (ratios 0.68-1.44, alternating jitter).

Family C, feather #87-#96 (10 lines, with outer #86):
- Near the narrow end, gaps about 0.92 (coefficient of variation 0.11, ratios 0.79-1.22). At 90%: gaps 2.93/2.76/2.82/3.92/4.47/5.32, growing outward (geometric 1.145/step, R2 0.85).
- At 50-60% there is a jump between lines 5 and 6 (1.17 -> 2.68), so two sub-groups.
- Free-end spacing 9.75/8.71/7.99/7.96/7.07/7.02/6.05/6.56/6.12, decreasing roughly linearly (about 0.93x per step).

Family D, curl fan #105-#110: gaps 3.8/4.4/3.3/2.3 at mid; endpoint spacing 8.7/6.3/6.8/5.8.
findings.phi_comparison: No family shows a phi progression. Spacing is roughly even with hand jitter of 10-40%, and successive gap ratios scatter from 0.7 to 1.5 around 1.0. Where there is a trend (feather C outer end, 1.14 per step; tendril tail, 0.81 per step), it is far from 1.618 and comes from lines fanning out from a shared convergence point.

findings.question: Q4: other structural relations in the medallion
findings.result:
- 62% of the 214 open stroke ends lie on another stroke. The anchors on the ellipse (cx 129.82, cy 130.63, rx 72.78, ry 70.06; rx/ry 1.039, an intended circle): tendrils #28-34 at its leftmost point; fan #55-60 at (173.6,186.6); #114 ends at the rightmost point (202.6,130.6); ring loops #40-#48 all end on the ellipse.
- Ring loops #40-#49 are near-copies of #43 (scale 0.85-1.06, RMS 0.004-1.4). They sit at radius 76-81 from the ellipse centre, with angular steps 24.0, 24.8, 31.0, 28.0, 31.6, 30.4, 25.8, 28.3, 27.9 deg (mean 28.0, coefficient of variation about 10%). #50-52 leave the ring and run down the stem; stem loops #99-102 are copies scaled 1.02-1.12.
- Scallops #12-#22 have an exact 9.00 pitch (copy-repeat); the last three, done by hand, are 7.74, 8.10, 8.63.
- Curls #1-#4 have lengths 57.07, 43.15, 31.72, 22.27 (ratios 1.32, 1.36, 1.42, not constant).
- #62-#65 are exact diagonal mirrors of #1-#4 (reflection plus 90 deg, RMS 0.00-0.03), so the corner has 45-deg mirror symmetry in places.
- Hatch lines #70-73 have lengths 8.27/5.66/3.99/2.26 (ratios 1.46/1.42/1.76).
- Piece w/h = 1.181.
findings.phi_comparison: Curl length ratios of about 1.37 fall between sqrt(phi)=1.272 and phi, and are not constant. Nothing else is close to phi. The strong, exact relations are copy/scale/mirror and snapping ends onto the circle; these are relational constraints, not phi constraints.

findings.question: Q3: crest proportions
findings.result:
- Exactly mirror-symmetric about x=854.91 (max control-point deviation 0.01).
- Overall bbox 87.57 x 47.77 (w/h 1.833).
- Axis features as a fraction of height from the top tip: inner tip 0.132, heart cusp 0.448, wing root 0.375, upper-heart bottom 0.630, wing tips 0.932, bottom 1.
- Inner upper heart #10 is an exact copy of outer heart #1 scaled by 0.7025 about the cusp (fixed point near (854.91,21.2)), RMS 0.003.
- Outer heart 37.22 x 30.08 (w/h 1.237); lower heart #0 26.95 x 26.36 (w/h 1.023), not a copy of either (RMS 2.7).
- Ratios: outer/lower heart width 1.381, height 1.141. Cusp depth ratio (top->cusp)/(cusp->bottom) = 0.812. Wing span / upper-heart width = 2.353.
- Wing hooks #7, #8, #9 are approximate scale copies (1.29, 1.22; RMS 2-3); their end offsets from the axis are 27.14, 30.88, 35.47.
findings.phi_comparison: The inner/outer heart scale of 0.7025 is 1/sqrt(2) (0.7071, 0.65% off), not 1/phi (12% off). Crest w/h 1.833 = phi^1.26 (11% from phi^1.5). The cusp ratio 0.812 vs phi^-0.5=0.786 (3.3%) and upper heart w/h 1.237 vs sqrt(phi) (2.7%) are within chance level. No convincing phi in the crest.

findings.question: Q3: side-leaf proportions
findings.result:
- The bottom half is an exact mirror of the top half about y=631.7 (RMS 0.18-0.23).
- bbox 62.17 x 243.74 (h/w 3.92); half-height 121.87.
- Leaf and lobe tip heights above the axis: 11.97 (#8), 26.88 (#13), 31.13 (#5), 52.92 (#6), 70.89 (#0 lobe). As fractions of half-height: 0.098, 0.221, 0.255, 0.434, 0.582.
- Successive ratios: 2.25, 1.16, 1.70, 1.34, 1.72 (to the half-height).
- All fan strokes converge at the socket (74.83,631.7).
findings.phi_comparison: h/w 3.92 = phi^2.84 (7% from phi^3). Tip fractions against phi^-n: 0.098 vs 0.090 (+9%), 0.255 vs 0.236 (+8%), 0.434 vs 0.382 (+14%), 0.582 vs 0.618 (-6%). Ratios jump between 1.16 and 2.25. No phi structure beyond chance.

implications: The drawings are not phi-governed now. Of all the measured ratios, only the flame tip curve comes near golden, and even there the best b is 0.49, not 0.306. The exact relations that do exist are Illustrator operations: similarity copies (flame leaves, crest hearts at 1/sqrt(2), ring loops), mirrors (crest, side-leaf, the diagonal in the medallion), exact repeats (scallop pitch 9.00) and snapping ends onto a circle. An engine should formalise these four operations (copy-along, scale-about, mirror, attach-to-curve) first and add phi as a parameter choice on top. The designer already works this way, which makes it realistic to design in.

Flame: rebuild it as one log-spiral 'spine' through the tips, with N leaves placed at equal angular steps. The leaf prototype gets scale proportional to spine radius and rotation equal to the spiral tangent angle plus a constant. With b=0.306 instead of the drawn 0.49, each tip moves about 1.6u RMS (max 2.4u) on a 119x209 piece, roughly 1-2% of the width and 3-5 stroke widths. That is visible on close comparison but keeps the same character; a free-pole golden fit moves the tips only 0.39 RMS (max 0.69u). The bigger visual change is the leaf sizes. They currently shrink linearly (1 -> 0.27); a self-similar rule would make them shrink geometrically, about 0.875 per 25-deg step at golden b, or 0.82 at b=0.49, so the smallest leaves would get noticeably larger.

Leaf shapes: each leaf side is one cubic with a mid-segment curvature peak, so no side is a log spiral. To get leaves that are 'perfectly golden', the engine has to generate each side as a log-spiral or clothoid arc (or a G2 spline with a prescribed curvature profile) and then fit cubics for SVG output. Snapping the existing control points will not do it. Measured local b of 0.21 (back) and 0.38/0.59 (front S) sit on either side of 0.306, so a golden leaf template is a plausible stylisation.

Medallion sweep: the S-curves are clothoids (curvature about linear in arc length, R2 0.98), and the ring part is a circle of radius about 1.2x the medallion radius. The natural 'dominant function' is therefore a circle-plus-Euler-spiral spline (as in Raph Levien's Spiro/Euler-spiral splines), not a golden spiral. Forcing a golden log spiral onto the limbs costs 1.3 RMS and 3.2u max with the wrong look. Phi can still set radii, for example ring radius = phi^k x medallion radius (it is 1.20 now; phi^0.5=1.27 would grow the ring about 5u), and the stem spacing (middle/outer gap 1.467 -> phi adds 1.7u).

Curls: the right scroll (#103) is a tight volute (b 0.14-0.16, about 2.5x growth per turn), and its inner part fits Archimedean equally well. A golden curl (6.85x per turn) is clearly more open; at the same outer size it shows about half as many turns. Expose 'turns' and 'b' as separate parameters, and let the designer choose golden b or a volute.

Nested line fans: the spacing is near-even with 10-40% jitter, and lines converge exactly on anchor points on the medallion circle. An engine can generate them as offsets or interpolations between two guide curves (Illustrator-blend-like), with a spacing law that is either uniform or geometric with ratio r. The drawn data supports uniform spacing (or r of about 1.1-1.15 at the open end), not r=phi; phi spacing (1.618 per step) would collapse the inner lines and look very different. The uniform/geometric choice should be a dial, not a hard-coded phi rule.

Because 62% of medallion stroke ends sit on other strokes (and fans sit on ellipse extremes and specific angles), the engine's core data model should be an attachment graph: each element is parameterised by the curve it hangs from (parameter t or angle on its parent) plus a local transform. Re-flowing to any page size then means moving the dominant curves, and the dependents follow.

Design workflow: the designer can keep drawing in Illustrator, with the engine fitting parameters back out, which is what these scripts do. Spiral pole and b, copy scale and rotation, mirror axis and attachment are all recoverable automatically, with residuals reported (copies at 0.003u, ring at 0.5u RMS). A 'fit then snap with a tolerance report' loop (for example 'snapping to golden moves tips 0.4-2.4u') is realistic. Note the look-elsewhere caveat: any ratio is within 12% of some half-power of phi, so the engine should impose phi by construction and not hunt for it in drawings.

verdicts.name: METAFONT / MetaPost (Knuth, Hobby): declarative equations + pens along paths
verdicts.note: WebFetch got a 403, but a direct download worked. The manual (by John D. Hobby) says '=' is not assignment but declares an equation; a=a+1 gives an 'inconsistent equation' error, and 'Redundant equation' is also reported. Linear equations may come in any order; z4=1/3[z3,z6] is the mediation example; z2r means (x2r,y2r). Bézier control points follow Hobby's 1986 spline (ref [7]), and pens are swept along paths (pickup pencircle, makepen, envelope). METAFONT dates 1979 and 1984 are consistent.

verdicts.name: Hobby's spline ('mock curvature') with a JS reference implementation
verdicts.note: The article covers Hobby's 1986 paper, 'continuity of mock curvature (a first-order approximation of true curvature)', linear-time computation and an ISC-licensed, heavily commented hobby.js. The technical details are in hobby.js (/blog/hobby-curves/hobby.js), not the article prose: chord lengths d[i], signed turning angles gamma[i], a tridiagonal system solved in O(n) with the Thomas algorithm for alpha, then beta and the rho velocity function. The article never mentions METAFONT, MetaPost or TikZ; the code comments name METAFONT. The TikZ hobby package exists separately. hobby.js handles open paths only (omega end curl).

verdicts.name: Raph Levien, 'From Spiral to Spline' (PhD 2009) and Spiro / libspiro
verdicts.note: UC Berkeley thesis (chair Carlo Séquin). It confirms the central result: any extensional, two-parameter spline has segments cut from a single generating curve, rotated, scaled and translated (Sec. 4.1). It calls the Euler spiral excellent all-round and adds that a log-aesthetic curve may be slightly better for some uses. libspiro is integrated into FontForge and Inkscape, and Levien designed several fonts entirely with these splines, including Inconsolata. XTrackCAD is not in the thesis; Levien's Spiro page (levien.com/spiro) names it.

verdicts.name: Log-aesthetic curves (Harada, Miura, Yoshida) and the golden spiral as a special case
verdicts.note: The paper is Nagy, Yoshida and Hoffmann, 'Interactive G1 and G2 Hermite Interpolation Using Extended Log-aesthetic Curves' (arXiv 2021; Computer-Aided Design and Applications 2022). It credits Harada et al. (LDDC approximated by straight lines) and Miura et al. (LCG, fundamental equation with slope alpha). It handles inflections and cusps and gives G2 joins through tangent-length control, and names the alpha=-1 clothoid and alpha=2 circle involute. It does not state alpha=0 Nielsen's spiral or alpha=1 logarithmic spiral; those are standard (Yoshida and Saito 2006). The golden spiral is one particular logarithmic spiral (alpha=1 with a fixed growth rate), not its own alpha value.

verdicts.name: Prototypo (Byte Foundry): browser-based parametric font engine
verdicts.note: The license is wrong: prototypo.js is GPL-3.0 (LICENSE file, package.json 'GPLv3'). MPL-2.0 covers .js/.jsx/.json files in the separate app repo byte-foundry/prototypo. The engine builds on the paper.js API and opentype.js through Byte Foundry's plumin.js dependency. The .ptf typefaces are separate CoffeeScript repos (byte-foundry/john-fell.ptf CC0, venus.ptf CC0, spectral.ptf OFL). The 'o' glyph data model is confirmed in john-fell.ptf src/glyphs/lowercases/o.coffee: skeleton:true, closed contours, nodes with x/y expressions over thickness, xHeight, width, contrast, overshoot and spacing, references like contours[0].nodes[2].expandedTo[0].x, dirOut, and expand {width, angle, distr}. The service was sunset on 1 July 2020, per Yannick Mathey's project page.

verdicts.name: OpenType variable fonts and Glyphs 'smart components'
verdicts.note: The spec (OpenType 1.9.1) confirms all of it. fvar min/default/max values map to -1/0/1, piecewise-linear and optionally remapped by avar. One default outline plus deltas, with point-compatible masters required. Regions are always rectilinear with a peak (and start/end for intermediate regions), and intermediate per-axis scalars are 'triangular'. Per-axis scalars are multiplied, and any out-of-range axis gives 0. Smart components are not on this page; glyphsapp.com/learn/smart-components confirms named properties interpolated with sliders.

verdicts.name: kurbo (Rust) and Levien and Uguray's Euler-spiral stroke expansion: fitting and offsetting
verdicts.note: docs.rs (v0.13.1) lists ParamCurveArclen, ParamCurveNearest, ParamCurveCurvature, the offset module, stroke/stroke_with, the simplify module, ParamCurveFit and fit_to_bezpath(_opt). The license is dual 'Apache-2.0 OR MIT', not Apache-2.0 alone. ParamCurveFit requires sample_pt_tangent, sample_pt_deriv and break_cusp, and uses area and moment integrals for fitting. The area plus x-moment quartic method is in Levien's 2021 post 'Fitting cubic Bézier curves' (raphlinus.github.io), not the docs. 'GPU-friendly Stroke Expansion' (Levien and Uguray, HPG 2024, arXiv 2405.00127) is confirmed and uses Euler spirals for parallel curves.

verdicts.name: paper.js, bezier.js and Pomax's 'A Primer on Bézier Curves' (JS curve toolkits)
verdicts.note: The Primer exists, is by Pomax, and uses Bezier.js for its interactive figures; it has sections on curvature, arc length and offsetting. paper.js Path docs confirm getPointAt, getTangentAt, getNormalAt and getCurvatureAt with offsets from 0 to path.length. smooth() types are 'continuous' (continuous first and second derivatives), 'asymmetric' (still the default for backward compatibility, to be removed), 'catmull-rom' (0 uniform, 0.5 centripetal 'guaranteeing no self-intersections', 1 chordal) and 'geometric' (tension 0-1). Licenses (paper.js MIT, bezier.js MIT) were not re-checked, but they match the known licenses.

verdicts.name: Nupuram (Santhosh Thottingal, 2025): a modern METAPOST type-design workflow
verdicts.note: The paper is titled 'Parametric type design in the era of variable and color fonts' (Jan 2025). It confirms METAPOST glyphs with Hobby paths and MetaType1's pen_stroke ('expanding stroke', a different pen per node). Output goes SVG to UFO to fontmake, with a VS Code live preview and a web proofing tool. Plain pencircle SVG output is only a stroked path, not a closed outline. METAFONT approximates pencircle with a 24-sided convex polygon for envelopes. The axes are wght, wdth, slnt and SOFT (four; the claim leaves out wdth). The abstract says 'two variable fonts'; Nupuram Calligraphy and Nupuram Color are subfamilies.

verdicts.name: Computer-Generated Floral Ornament (Wong, Zongker & Salesin, SIGGRAPH 1998) - 'adaptive clip art'
verdicts.note: The PDF confirms it. Adaptive clip art is elements plus growth rules and can be regenerated when the region changes. Each element type has one or more proxies (circle, arc, bezier, linesegment, etc.) and user fields. Proxies are used only to find empty space and test intersections, and a separate render procedure draws the final art. Rule bodies are C++ code (a Perl preprocessor generates C++, with about 3,600 lines of C++ framework). Rendering in several styles uses skeletal strokes. SIGGRAPH '98 is confirmed by citations (pp. 423-434).

verdicts.name: FLOWPAK: Flow-based Ornamental Element Packing (Saputra, Kaplan, Asente, Měch, Graphics Interface 2017)
verdicts.note: The PDF confirms it. One colour-coded diagram holds black boundaries (containers), red direction guides with arrows and green fixed elements copied verbatim. Each element must have a straight spine and is classed as full (both sides) or half (one side). The LR function samples how far the element extends left and right of the spine at n points, normalised to [0,1]. The vector field comes from guide tangents (N-RoSy), streamlines are traced Jobard-Lefer style, and elements are placed as skeletal strokes along them.

verdicts.name: Magnetic Curves: Curvature-Controlled Aesthetic Curves Using Magnetic Fields (Xu & Mould, CAe 2009)
verdicts.note: Confirmed: Computational Aesthetics 2009. Lorentz force F = qv × B with B along z keeps motion in the xy plane, integrated by forward Euler. Radius r = mv/(qB), so a higher q gives a tighter curve. The profile is q(t) = (T - t)^-alpha, where T sets length and alpha the rate (examples T = 650, 450, 250, 50 and alpha = 0.8 to 0.65). Examples include space-filling branching curves, a stylised tree after Klimt's Tree of Life, hair, two window frames and cartoon flames (with a charge reversal). 'Ornamental scroll fields' loosely describes the space-filling examples.

verdicts.name: The Deco Framework for Interactive Procedural Modeling (Měch & Miller, JCGT 2012) - shipped as Flash Pro CS4-CS6 Deco tools and in Photoshop CS6
verdicts.note: Confirmed (JCGT vol. 1 no. 1, 2012; http redirects to https). Deco shipped in Flash Pro CS4 to CS6 and Photoshop CS6. Scriptals are JavaScript files defining modules with produce(), environment<Name>() and render(), and the engine runs repeated produce, environment and render passes over a linked list of modules. Environments are dynamically loaded C++ libraries, for example Collision, where a module renders into the environment and is removed if it collides. The paper names the CS4 tools spray brush, flower-fill (shown as Vine Fill in Flash's UI), grid-fill and symmetry; CS5 added seven tools including tree, flower and lightning brushes.

verdicts.name: Skeletal Strokes (Hsu, Lee & Wiseman, UIST 1993) plus Asente's folding-avoidance and automatic corner-tile patents (Adobe)
verdicts.note: Despite its filename, the PDF is the UIST '93 paper 'Skeletal Strokes' (Hsu, Lee, Wiseman); it is not the SIGGRAPH '94 'Drawing and animation using skeletal strokes'. It confirms flesh defined against a reference backbone (x-axis) and a reference thickness (lateral scale), mapped onto any path with stretching, bending and shearing, and that naive normal-based mapping can fold. The word 'rib' is not in this paper; it comes from Asente's patents. Those patents exist: US 8,674,995 'Folding avoidance in skeletal stroke application' and US 8,941,661 'Automatic corner generation' (pattern-brush corner tiles from side tiles), both Adobe and both by Asente. There is also his SBIM 2010 paper 'Folding Avoidance in Skeletal Strokes'.

verdicts.name: Islamic Star Patterns from Polygons in Contact (Kaplan, GI 2005) and Taprats rendering styles (Kaplan, Bridges 2000 / VisMath)
verdicts.note: PDF text confirms the claims. Rays leave the edge midpoints at the contact angle and form an X. Trying every pairing would cost on the order of n! partitions of the 2n rays, so the paper uses a greedy pairing instead. Section 3.1 'Islamic parquet deformations' varies the contact angle along a line, e.g. 22.5 deg at the sides to 67.5 deg in the middle. Decoration uses the Taprats styles (ref [17], Bridges 2000). The Kaplan 2000 paper (cs.uwaterloo.ca/~csk/publications/Papers/kaplan_2000.pdf) lists Plain, Outline, Emboss, Interlace and Checkerboard (Fig. 7), with the descriptions the claim gives. Small nuance: the parquet deformations ran as a slow command-line tool, not in the interactive app.

verdicts.name: Celtic knot / interlace construction: Mercat's medial-graph method, Gross & Tucker's Celtic framework, Wackrill's gcd rule, Kaplan & Cohen's rendering
verdicts.note: The Klein Project article by Mercat and Artigue supports the steps. It says to draw a cross at each edge midpoint, inclined 30-60 deg to the edge, then follow walls (edges) through doors (crossings) and decide over/under. Gross and Tucker exist, 'A Celtic Framework for Knots and Links', DCG 46:86-99, published 2011 (online 2010). The paper supports the 2m x 2n grid with construction dots at points where x+y is odd, and the barriers. Kaplan and Cohen, 'Computer Generated Celtic Design', EGWR 2003, exists. 'Wackrill' could not be found in any source. The gcd rule itself is real (strands in a p x q panel = gcd(p,q)) but is documented by Fisher and Mellor, 'On the Topology of Celtic Knot Designs', Bridges 2004, and by entrelacs.net. The 'Wackrill' attribution looks wrong or unverifiable.

verdicts.name: DecoBrush: Drawing Structured Decorative Patterns by Example (Lu, Barnes, Wan, Asente, Měch, Finkelstein, SIGGRAPH 2014)
verdicts.note: Paper text confirms all the details. Each library has 8-12 strokes in one consistent style. Exemplars are rasterised at 512x512, with an optional SDF. The user marks the start and end of the main branch. The spine is found by Dijkstra on the pixel grid following edge tangent flow, then fitted with a quartic polynomial. Strokes are uv-parameterised with 30-100 samples. At runtime, piecewise matching (from Lu et al. 2013) is followed by graph cuts, texture synthesis and vectorisation, done in Illustrator for SDF outputs.

verdicts.name: Owen Jones, The Grammar of Ornament (1856): General Principles (37 propositions) and chapter analyses
verdicts.note: Propositions 6 (lines growing out of one another in gradual undulations, no excrescences), 7 (general forms, then general lines, then interstices subdivided 'for closer inspection') and 8 (geometrical construction) are confirmed verbatim. Caveat: this archive.org copy's OCR only contains Propositions 1-18, apparently because pages are missing. The book does have 37 propositions (Prop. 37 on art education, confirmed elsewhere). The chapter texts do restate 'radiation from the parent stem' and 'tangential curvature' in the Egyptian and Moresque chapters, among others.

verdicts.name: Lewis F. Day (The Anatomy of Pattern 1887; Nature in Ornament 1892) and Christopher Dresser (Principles of Decorative Design 1873) on skeletons, growth lines, curves and proportion
verdicts.note: The URL is Day's The Anatomy of Pattern (Batsford, 1887). These quotes are confirmed: 'lines inevitable to its consistency', 'the skeleton or framework upon which you build up your pattern', 'Pattern is a vertebrate thing; and in a scroll the spinal cord is very decidedly pronounced', 'clothe it, as nature does' and 'The spiral itself is only a series of segments of circles'. Day also says you have not done away with construction by keeping the scaffolding out of sight. The Dresser and Nature in Ornament parts were not checked at this URL.

verdicts.name: Designer-control research: Gieseke et al. 'Organized Order in Ornamentation' (CAe 2017) and 'A Survey of Control Mechanisms for Creative Pattern Generation' (CGF 2021); PATEX (Guerrero et al. 2016)
verdicts.note: The Purdue page lists the CGF 2021 survey (Gieseke, Asente, Mech, Benes, Fuchs; DOI 10.1111/cgf.142658) but carries no abstract. The CAe 2017 abstract (diglib.eg.org 10.2312/cae2017a04) confirms combinable placement functions under global constraints (balance, symmetry), strokes for connectivity and hierarchy, guides that make vector fields followed as streamlines, and path planning that routes around obstacles. PATEX (Guerrero, Bernstein, Li, Mitra; SIGGRAPH/TOG 2016) confirms multiple regularity interpretations surfaced as suggested edits.

verdicts.name: D'Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1917): gnomon theorem and the theory of transformations
verdicts.note: Gutenberg #55264 is the 1917 edition. It has Ch. XI 'The Logarithmic Spiral', Ch. XIV 'On Leaf-Arrangement, or Phyllotaxis' and Ch. XVII 'On the Theory of Transformations'. The text gives the Hero/Aristotle definition of the gnomon and states the three propositions as summarised: (1) log spirals through corresponding points; (2) each increment is a gnomon to the pre-existing structure; (3) other gnomonic figures can be inscribed only as a 'mathematical accident'.

verdicts.name: Theodore Andrea Cook, The Curves of Life (1914)
verdicts.note: Archive item is Cook's The Curves of Life (1914). On p. 420: 'Mr. Mark Barr suggested to Mr. Schooling that this ratio should be called the phi proportion', partly after Pheidias. It shows the 'double Fibonacci series' phi^2 = 1+phi, phi^3 = 1+2phi, ... and gives Church's 'ideal angle' 137 deg 30' 27.95" as 2pi/phi^2. The Colman critique (pp. 433-435) matches: Colman treats departures from 'extreme and mean proportion' as negligible, while Cook says the deviations matter more.

verdicts.name: George Markowsky, 'Misconceptions about the Golden Ratio', College Mathematics Journal 23(1), 1992
verdicts.note: The PDF is a JSTOR download (canonical: jstor.org/stable/2686193) of CMJ 23(1):2-19, 1992. It confirms the claims: an assumed +/-1% measurement error gives about +/-2% in a ratio, and the 'acceptance range' is 1.58-1.66, which is necessary but not proof. It says spirals can be built from rectangles of any ratio other than 1:1 (Fig. 3b uses sqrt2:1) and cites Thompson pp. 181-187.

verdicts.name: John Sharp, 'Spirals and the Golden Section', Nexus Network Journal 4(1), 2002
verdicts.note: The URL is Part 4 ('The Myth of the Nautilus Shell') of a multi-part article. Its table matches: rectangle 72.9676 deg / phi^4 = 6.8541; LLS 75.6788 / phi^(10/3) = 4.9731; SSL 79.1609 / phi^(5/2) = 3.3302; pentagon 62.9520 / phi^(20/3) = 24.7315. It also states all the spirals are logarithmic and differ in tangent angle. The nautilus measurements over 360 deg were 2.95, 3.02, 2.83 and 2.97 (average 2.94, about 3, tangent 80.08 deg), which does not match the golden rectangle spiral. The per-90/108/144/54 deg forms are correct derivations.

verdicts.name: Ronald Hübner, 'Golden spiral or Fibonacci spiral: Which is more beautiful and why?' (2024)
verdicts.note: Published in i-Perception 15(2), 2024. It confirms N=106 online, a golden spiral of 3.038 turns against a Fibonacci spiral of 11 quarter circles (2.75 turns), and an Archimedean spiral of 5 turns against a Dürer spiral of 10 half circles. 79.2% preferred the golden spiral and 81.1% the Archimedean. The paper explains this by continuous curvature against stepwise curvature.

verdicts.name: Renaissance compass volutes: Serlio, Salviati, Philandrier/Dürer (Andrey & Galli 2004), Goldmann's volute (Vollrath), and a programmatic re-implementation (Menezes Leitão)
verdicts.note: Andrey and Galli, 'Geometric Methods of the 1500s for Laying Out the Ionic Volute', Nexus Network Journal 6(2), 2004. Confirmed points: they redrew Serlio, Salviati and Philandrier and plotted the radius increments; each turn of the Serlio and Salviati volutes is like a truncated Archimedean spiral (three per volute); Salviati diminishes by 1/2 unit per quarter turn, then 1/3, then 1/6; and the paper notes Salviati's reflections on curvature discontinuity at the transitions between turns. Philandrier follows Dürer's point-based construction. The Goldmann/Vollrath and Menezes Leitão parts were not checked at this URL.

verdicts.name: Vogel's sunflower model, the golden angle, the three-gap theorem and golden-ratio low-discrepancy sequences
verdicts.note: MathWorld gives r_n = c*sqrt(n) and theta_n = n*alpha, with alpha = pi(3 - sqrt5) as the golden angle. It says the points satisfy Fermat's spiral and cites Vogel, Math. Biosci. 44:179-189 (1979). MathWorld does not discuss angle sensitivity, but ThatsMaths (2014-06-05) says verbatim: 'If the angle is even one degree too small or too large, the pattern is broken.' The golden-angle and three-gap statements are standard and correct.

verdicts.name: Raph Levien: the Euler spiral history, 'From Spiral to Spline' (Spiro), and Euler-spiral parallel curves
verdicts.note: The URL is Levien's PhD thesis (UCB/EECS-2009-162, Dec 2009). It covers interpolating splines through on-curve points, the extensional requirement, Euler-spiral generating curves, and G2 and G4 variants (Ch. 7, which trades G4 against locality). The companion history is a separate report, UCB/EECS-2008-111, which covers Bernoulli, Euler, Fresnel and Talbot. Talbot's 1890 'Railway Transition Spiral' is quoted there: 'degree-of-curve increases directly as the distance along the curve'. Use in FontForge and Inkscape was not re-verified here but is well known.

verdicts.name: B. de Smit & H. W. Lenstra Jr., 'The Mathematical Structure of Escher's Print Gallery' (Notices AMS, 2003)
verdicts.note: PDF loads: Notices AMS vol. 50 no. 4, April 2003. The text confirms the straight picture is invariant under scaling by 256 (f(256z)=f(z), from a factor of 4 per corner study, 4^4=256), that it is pulled back by the complex exponential into a doubly periodic picture, the map h(w)=w^gamma with gamma=(2πi+log 256)/(2πi), and the self-copy 'rotated clockwise by 157.6255960832... degrees and scaled down by a factor of 22.5836845286'. The paper backs the conformality-keeps-squares-square point by quoting Ernst: 'the original squares could better retain their square appearance'.

verdicts.name: Victorian design grammar: Owen Jones, The Grammar of Ornament (1856), Propositions 8-13, and Christopher Dresser, Principles of Decorative Design (1873)
verdicts.note: Gutenberg #39749 is Dresser's Principles of Decorative Design (4th edition; the page gives no original year), not Jones, so this URL covers only the Dresser half. I checked the Jones propositions against a scan of the original text and against readingdesign.org/grammar-of-ornament, and all match. Prop 8: geometrical construction. Prop 9: definite proportions on a simple unit, '4 to 8 less beautiful than the more subtle ratio of 5 to 8'. Prop 10: straight, inclined and curved. Prop 11: parent stem, branch and root. Prop 12: tangential junctions. Prop 13: conventionalise natural forms. The Dresser part of the claim is cut off, so I could not check it.

verdicts.name: Proportional scales as designer tools: Tim Brown's modular scale (A List Apart, 2011) and Le Corbusier's Modulor
verdicts.note: Tim Brown, 'More Meaningful Typography', A List Apart, 3 May 2011. The article confirms ratio x base multiplied and divided (10 gives 16.18, 26.18, 6.18, 3.82), double-stranded scales with two ratios or bases, 'comment math', and 'Modular scales are a tool, they're not magic.' The ALA article does not mention Le Corbusier or the Modulor, so that half needs its own source. The red/blue series claim agrees with standard accounts of the Modulor, but I did not check it here.

verdicts.name: Harriss spiral (Edmund Harriss; Chalkdust magazine)
verdicts.note: The page confirms the plastic ratio ≈1.3247 as the real root of x^3=x+1, a plastic rectangle splitting into a square plus two smaller plastic rectangles, and two arcs per square chosen to line up with the arcs in the sub-rectangles. As the claim says, it gives no exact radii or centres.

verdicts.name: Digital Facial Engraving (Victor Ostromoukhov, SIGGRAPH 99)
verdicts.note: PDF (12 MB) is the SIGGRAPH 99 paper. It confirms layers built from 'uniformly spaced waves' on a unit square in uv whose cross-section has a 'simple saw shape' modelled on the triangular furrows. It also confirms the 'universal' copperplate as a threshold matrix ('nothing other than conventional dithering'), warping via Coons patches drawn in Illustrator, and merging modes (copy/smaller/bigger etc.) with range shift/scale masks. Fig. 1 shows stamp and banknote engravings. 'Base reference for security and stamp printing' is the summary's own judgement and is not stated in the paper.

verdicts.name: Artistic Halftoning – Between Technology and Art (Ostromoukhov, SPIE 2000; covers Artistic Screening SIGGRAPH 95 and Multicolor/Artistic Dithering SIGGRAPH 99)
verdicts.note: The abstract covers Artistic Screening (SIGGRAPH95), Multicolor and Artistic Dithering (SIGGRAPH99) and Digital Facial Engraving. Supported by the text: predefined contours drawn in Adobe Illustrator; cubic Bézier control polygons, with straight parts also stored as Bézier polygons; shape blending to 256 levels (z=0,1/255,…); scan conversion with the non-zero winding rule; separate definition and rendition spaces using conformal maps; microlettering and an 'imaginary banknote' against desktop counterfeiting.

verdicts.name: DigiDürer – a digital engraving system (Pnueli & Bruckstein, The Visual Computer 1994)
verdicts.note: Visual Computer (1994) 10:277-292. The text lists the three properties (nonintersecting, approximately parallel, smooth except at edges), which are characteristic of equipotential lines. It also confirms 'local density of halftone lines in the direction normal to the lines... proportional to the local gray level', the Eikonal equation with initial line L(s,0) as the boundary condition, and contours sampled ΔH apart with ΔH proportional to line width w.

verdicts.name: Rose engine & straightline engine guilloché (G. Phil Poirier, SNAG Technical Article Part 2, 2016)
verdicts.note: SNAG Technical Article, April 2016, Part 2 by G. Phil Poirier. Confirmed: the headstock is spring-loaded so the rosette rocks against a fixed Touch, and cutting runs from outside to centre one increment per cut. One rosette gives hundreds or thousands of patterns. Concentric is the simplest. A half-pitch shift turns a 24-lobe rosette 1/48 of a circle (7.5°) for Barleycorn. 1° per cut gives Pinwheel (Fig 37), and Fig 38 uses 1° for 5 cuts then reverses. The article also covers how the ratio of touch radius to lobe radius changes the cut shape.

verdicts.name: Envelope-based guilloche rosettes and borders (Stephen M. Cameron, 'Playing Around With Guilloche Patterns' slides + Processing code) with the Variable Guilloche patent US8289579B2
verdicts.note: The URL is one slide (17) of a series running talk0 to talk24. Across the series: spirograph wheels along a path (3-14). Slide 16 gives the undulating circle r = cos(t*C*M)*R + min_radius. Slide 17 maps a sinusoid scaled to -0.5..+0.5, +0.5, × envelope difference + inner, with two curves π/2 out of phase. Slide 18 has N curves offset by 1/N of a circle, slide 19 a 7-pointed star envelope, and slide 20 uses an outer envelope as the next rosette's inner. The GitHub repo is MIT-licensed Processing (.pde). Patent US8289579B2 ('Variable guilloche and method', HP) lists eight polar curve families: cardioids, roses, limaçons, lemniscates, spirals, conchoids, elliptic and hyperbolic conics.

verdicts.name: Commercial security-design software: Agfa Arziro Design (Illustrator plug-in) and Jura Corvina / Corvina Engraver (Lupo specimen banknote)
verdicts.note: The Jura page lists Corvina Prime/Plus and Corvina Engraver ('designed to emulate classic engraving techniques') plus DLE intaglio platemaking. It does not mention Arziro, Lupo or guilloche. The Arziro modules come from Agfa's product page (CAPTCHA-blocked for me; I relied on search summaries of it and on PrintWeek): an Illustrator plug-in for Mac/PC with Special Rasters (Line/Select/Trafo/Dither), Special Reliefs (Quick Background, Numismatics), Crystal Patterns, Path Definition, Line/Object Generator, a Guilloche Library & Generator (v4.0), and predefined or custom parameters. Keesing's Lupo article confirms Jura used its Corvina suite and 'digitally engraved' the wolf portrait in vector form for the 2015 Lupo specimen.

verdicts.name: Evenly-spaced streamlines (Jobard & Lefer 1997) and anvaka/streamlines (JavaScript implementation)
verdicts.note: The repo is MIT-licensed, follows the Jobard paper and uses RK4. In index.js, dTest defaults to dSep*0.5 and createLookupGrid(boundingBox, dSep) builds a uniform grid with cell size dSep. The README example uses dSep 0.5 and dTest 0.25. The Jobard & Lefer 1997 abstract (VisSym '97) describes outputs 'ranging from texture-like to hand-drawing styles', so the hand-drawing quote checks out.

verdicts.name: Computer-Generated Pen-and-Ink Illustration (Winkenbach & Salesin, SIGGRAPH 94)
verdicts.note: Appendix A.3.1 confirms the stroke model: path P(u) for the overall 'sweep', nib N(p) as the footprint versus pressure, and character function C(u)=(Cw waviness, Cp pressure), combined by convolution. The C++ InkPen is made of a Nib, a WavinessFunction and a PressureFunction. Tone: total stroke length vA/w. Cross-hatching: 2x − x² = v. The paper also has prioritized stroke textures and resolution-dependent rendering (Fig. 3).

verdicts.name: Real-Time Halftoning: A Primitive for Non-Photorealistic Shading (Freudenberg, Masuch, Strothotte, EGWR 2002)
verdicts.note: Thirteenth Eurographics Workshop on Rendering 2002. Confirmed: a binary threshold aliases and pops, and the smooth threshold 'tmp = add(1 - tex, -col) * C; out = 1 - tmp' with 'the value 4 useful', clamped to 0..1 by the hardware, antialiases. The screen is applied in texture space per pixel. A 1D gray-ramp texture is enough for a single set of parallel engraving lines. The paper cites Ostromoukhov's dither screens, and its prioritized stroke textures are inspired by Winkenbach & Salesin.

verdicts.name: Browser print-simulation toolkit: SVG ink-gain/letterpress filters, variable-width outlines, and their performance limits
verdicts.note: The article confirms ink gain (feMorphology dilate radius=2 on SourceAlpha, merged under SourceGraphic), thinning by erode (radius 1), and worn letterpress (feTurbulence fractalNoise, baseFrequency 0.035, numOctaves 3, into feDisplacementMap scale 6). On cost it gives qualitative guidance: 'Filters are not free', with turbulence, displacement and lighting the expensive ones. It does NOT contain the Andy Jakubowski ink-bleed recipe (blur + feComponentTransfer feFuncA discrete '0 1 1 1'), and I could not find any source for that attribution. Its 'ink bleed' demo uses feTurbulence. The article also does not cover variable-width lines in SVG, so those parts need other sources.

verdicts.name: Illustrator-native guilloche construction (Envato Tuts+ 'Create a Security Seal in Illustrator Using Guilloche Patterns')
verdicts.note: Page loads and every checked number matches. Oval at 0.25 pt stroke (80% black), rotated 2° and repeated with Cmd+D to 360°. Star with 36 points and 20 px rounded corners, blended with a 50%-scaled copy at 30 steps, then appearance expanded. 36 lines at 10° plus a group copy rotated 5°. Stacked lines with Effect > Distort & Transform > Zig Zag, clipped into an outlined 'V' (Cmd+7). Text on a circle path is set in Times New Roman Bold. Minor: the clip shape is a single letter 'V', not 'letterforms' in general.

verdicts.name: CSS Houdini Paint API: the spec, houdini.how worklets, Temani Afif's polygon border and the Paint Flecks worklet used on CSS-Tricks
verdicts.note: The spec confirms registerPaint(), paint(ctx, size, styleMap, args), and that paint() works anywhere an <image> is accepted. MDN confirms PaintRenderingContext2D is a subset that excludes CanvasImageData, CanvasUserInterface, CanvasText and CanvasTextDrawingStyles. The houdini.how repo (GoogleChromeLabs, archived May 2024) lists angled-corners and extra-scalloped by Una, border-radius-reverse by Surma, and paint-flecks. Temani Afif's 'Polygon Border' Paint API article exists on dev.to and CSS-Tricks. CodePen Radio ep. 340 (2021) confirms CSS-Tricks used George's paint worklet in its header and footer. Caveats: (1) houdini.how now 301-redirects to an unrelated site (techgory.com), so link the GitHub repo instead. (2) Paint Flecks was designed by George Francis; the npm package houdini-paint-flecks is by Jake Archibald. (3) The API is Chromium-only natively (Safari partial, Firefox none).

verdicts.name: Rough.js (RoughGenerator) and Excalidraw's ShapeCache
verdicts.note: The RoughGenerator wiki page (/wiki/RoughGenerator) confirms the following. A drawable holds instructions only and is serializable to JSON. toPaths(drawable) returns PathInfo {d, stroke, strokeWidth, fill, pattern}, which must be rendered in order (only one of fill or pattern is set). rough.generator(config, {width, height}) works without a canvas, e.g. in a background worker or on a server. Excalidraw source (packages/element/src/shape.ts) defines class ShapeCache with a static RoughGenerator and a WeakMap cache keyed by element, so the claim holds. The wiki root URL itself covers the generator only briefly; the details are on the RoughGenerator subpage.

verdicts.name: Rough Notation and Wired Elements (Preet Shihn): procedural SVG redrawn as page elements resize
verdicts.note: Checked against src/rough-notation.ts. The SVG gets position:absolute, overflow:visible and pointer-events:none. It is inserted with insertAdjacentElement('beforebegin') for highlight and 'afterend' otherwise, and the target is set to relative positioning for highlights. The code adds a window 'resize' listener and a ResizeObserver on the target. A 400 ms setTimeout gate means one check per window. It redraws via show() only if haveRectsChanged() is true. Wired Elements is confirmed as 'built using RoughJS and Lit'. Its WiredBase extends LitElement, clears and redraws an inline SVG in draw() whenever the measured size changes, and uses a random seed per instance.

verdicts.name: Paper.js and Bezier.js: curve geometry kernels (arc-length queries, offsets, graduated outlines)
verdicts.note: The Paper.js Path reference matches. The length property is described as 'approximate'. The page documents getPointAt, getTangentAt, getNormalAt, getCurvatureAt (radius is the reciprocal), getLocationAt, getOffsetOf (returns null when the point is off the path) and getOffsetsWithTangent. smooth() types: 'continuous' (continuous 1st/2nd derivatives), 'asymmetric' (the default, deprecated), 'catmull-rom' (factor 0 uniform, 0.5 centripetal, 1 chordal) and 'geometric' (tension factor, default 0.4). Bezier.js (pomax.github.io/bezierjs) has offset(d), outline(d1,d2,d3,d4) for graduated outlines, length() by Legendre-Gauss quadrature, curvature(t) returning k and r, reduce() and arcs().

verdicts.name: perfect-freehand (Steve Ruiz): centerline to variable-width outline polygon
verdicts.note: The README confirms the following. getStroke returns the outline polygon. getStrokePoints returns {point, pressure, vector, distance, runningLength}, and getStrokeOutlinePoints consumes that. Options are size, thinning (negative values thin the stroke as pressure rises), smoothing, streamline, simulatePressure, easing, start/end {cap, taper, easing} and last. Pressure is passed as [x, y, p] or {pressure}, and the README links a Figma plugin. Source: radius = size * easing(0.5 - thinning*(0.5 - pressure)). The README does not mention tldraw. tldraw ships an adapted copy of the code (packages/tldraw/src/lib/shapes/shared/freehand), so 'used in tldraw' is true in substance.

verdicts.name: canvas-sketch and canvas-sketch-util/penplot (Matt DesLauriers)
verdicts.note: physical-units.md confirms the following. dimensions can be an array or a preset ('A4', 'letter', 'arch-2'). orientation and pixelsPerInch (default 72) are settings. bleed adds 2x bleed. trimWidth and trimHeight give the trim size, and the exporting flag is used to skip drawing the trim guide. The canvas is scaled to fit the window while units stay physical. Cmd/Ctrl+S exports at print resolution (a 3.5x2 in card exports at 1050x600 px at 300 PPI). The units list 'in','cm','px','ft','m','mm' and the 'postcard' preset come from api.md and lib/paper-sizes.js, not this page. canvas-sketch-util/penplot confirms plotter-ready SVG via pathsToSVG.

verdicts.name: Tyler Hobbs, 'Flow Fields' essay: one dominant field that every line follows
verdicts.note: The essay confirms the following. The grid gets an example 50% extra margin outside the image. He writes that he 'usually' uses ~0.5% of image width for resolution, but the pseudocode uses int(width*0.01), i.e. 1%. Step length is ~0.1–0.5% of width. Curves follow cell angles for num_steps, and at each step the curve stops if another curve is too close. The essay gives no numeric value for num_steps or the collision distance. Fidenza appears only as a related-reading link, though Hobbs is indeed Fidenza's artist.

verdicts.name: {Shan, Shui}* (Lingdong Huang): procedurally generated, infinitely scrolling SVG Chinese landscape scroll
verdicts.note: Checked against index.html. parseArgs reads ?seed= and defaults to SEED = new Date().getTime(). A custom Prng (Blum-Blum-Shub style squaring mod p*q) replaces Math.random globally, so a seed reproduces the output. mountplanner(xmin, xmax) emits {tag, x, y, h} placements from Perlin-noise local maxima (locmax) and tracks occupancy in MEM.planmtx. chunkloader then turns each plan into SVG chunks per 512-unit chunk. Minor omission: mountplanner also emits 'boat' tags, not only mount, distmount and flatmount.

verdicts.name: Rive: Follow Path constraint and Layout fit, a designer-authored constraint runtime on the web
verdicts.note: The docs confirm Strength, Target, Distance (a percentage that 'can exceed 100%'), Orient (manual rotation disabled when on) and Offset. The runtime source is in rive-app/rive-runtime (formerly rive-cpp), at src/constraints/follow_path_constraint.cpp. update() collects every Path of a target Shape into one RawPath and measures it (m_pathMeasure). targetTransform uses atPercentage(distance) for position and tangent, and blends rotation and position by strength(). Layout fit was not checked because that part of the claim was truncated.

verdicts.name: Generative identity systems: MIT Media Lab 2011 (TheGreenEyl and E Roon Kang), the Pentagram 2014 grid system, and the Stripe.dev 'design instrument'
verdicts.note: MIT 2011 (CAN) is supported: a Processing app moves 3 shapes on a 4x4-square grid under rules that they hit the boundaries and intersect, giving 40,000 logos x 12 color combinations, about 480,000 total. Pentagram's page confirms the ML monogram and a glyph system for 23 groups built on the previous anniversary logo's 'seven-by-seven grid'. The page gives no year; 2014 is correct from other knowledge. Note the 4x4 (CAN) vs 7x7 (Pentagram) grid descriptions conflict between sources. Stripe is overstated: the Awwwards case study says purely content-generated art 'lacked a human touch', so they built a design instrument (stripe.dev/art) to 'play' the possibility space and hand-produce several dozen pieces. 'The same simple math' cycles the accent colors. Neither the art nor the colors are generated from content.

verdicts.name: Penrose (CMU): ensure/encourage constraint styling with optimization
verdicts.note: The page confirms SIGGRAPH 2020 (ACM TOG 39(4)) by Ye, Ni, Krieger, Ma'ayan, Wise, Aldrich, Sunshine and Crane. Diagrams are generated by 'constrained numerical optimization' from .dsl, .sub and .sty programs, and there is a web IDE. The Penrose wiki says constraints are used via ensure and objectives via encourage. Source (packages/core Constraints.ts and Objectives.ts) contains contains, disjoint, onCanvas, lessThan (with a padding arg) and equal as constraints, and near, notTooClose, sameCenter, above and below as objectives. The siggraph20 page alone does not define ensure vs encourage; the docs and source do.

verdicts.name: Modular Scale and Utopia: ratio-based proportional systems enforced across a site and across viewport sizes
verdicts.note: modularscale.com confirms Tim Brown and Scott Kellum, the '1:1.618 – golden section' preset, ms(0) usage in Sass and JS, and the point that two bases plus two ratios 'would really dilute the scale' (phrased as an explanation rather than a formal warning). Utopia's 'Designing with fluid type scales' post defines a 1.2 scale at 320px and a 1.333 scale at 1500px, interpolated by viewport. The clamp post shows the clamp() interpolation (e.g. clamp(1rem, 0.7143rem + 1.4286vw, 2rem)). The cited clamp URL covers the interpolation mechanics. The two-scale definition is in the separate designing-with-fluid-type-scales post.

verdicts.name: Grasshopper for Rhino (curve parameters, Perp Frames, Graph Mapper, referenced Rhino curves)
verdicts.note: The site describes Grasshopper as 'a graphical algorithm editor tightly integrated with Rhino's 3-D modeling tools' that 'requires no knowledge of programming or scripting'. It has shipped built into Rhino since Rhino 6. On grasshopper3d.com forum threads, David Rutten says Reparameterize only sets the domain to 0~1 and does not change shape, and that equidistant spacing 'has nothing to do with parameterization', so t=0.5 is not the length midpoint. Divide Curve, Perp Frames and Graph Mapper are standard components; their specific details were truncated in the claim and were not individually checked.

verdicts.name: Daniel Davis, 'Modelled on Software Engineering' (PhD thesis, RMIT 2013)
verdicts.note: Chapter 6 page confirms all of these: 2,002 models, 97.5% with no modules (clusters), 48% with no structure (groups, text or named branches), and 81% with no uniquely named parameters. In the think-aloud test (4 students), all could explain the structured model's function, and none correctly guessed the unstructured one. Chapter 1 (danieldavis.com/thesis-ch1/) has the Gerber quote 'generally needs to be remade' (2007). Burry (1996) is quoted as 'completely disassemble the model and restart at the critical decision', but only for when a critical change is made.

verdicts.name: Inkscape Live Path Effects: Pattern Along Path, Power Stroke
verdicts.note: The source matches. It calls arc_length_parametrization(path_i,2,0.1) and computes n = rot90(derivative(uskeleton)). The output is compose(uskeleton,x+offs)+y*compose(n,x+offs). The four copy types (Single, Single stretched, Repeated, Repeated stretched) exist. In 'Repeated, stretched' the copy count is floored with a minimum of 1, and the pattern is scaled so the copies fill the skeleton length (open paths also subtract the spacing). I did not separately check the Power Stroke or original-d/d storage details.

verdicts.name: Adobe Illustrator pattern brushes and art brushes
verdicts.note: The page exists. It is a video tutorial covering side, corner, start and end tiles and the three fit options, and it mentions auto-generated corners only in general terms ('auto in between'). The four auto-corner names (Auto-Centered, Auto-Between, Auto-Sliced, Auto-Overlap) and their descriptions are correct, but they come from other sources such as Peachpit. One correction: Adobe's own help describes Approximate Path as fitting tiles to the closest approximate path without changing the tiles, placing them slightly inside or outside the path to keep tiling even. It does not edit the path object. 'Changes the path itself' is a third-party paraphrase. Adobe's helpx brush page returned 403 when fetched, so the Adobe wording above comes from memory, not a live read.

verdicts.name: Glyphs app smart components, corner and cap components, segment components and brushes
verdicts.note: The handbook confirms the following. Properties have a minimum and maximum. Smart layers drawn at the extremes must be compatible with the master. Values are interpolated, and also extrapolated (with a warning that this can look poor). Missing combinations are inferred from the single-property layers. Separate handbook pages (/components/corner/, /cap/, /segment/) confirm that corner components sit on a node, cap components on two nodes, and segment components and brushes bend along path segments.

verdicts.name: Sketch-n-Sketch (UIST 2016; UIST 2019)
verdicts.note: The paper (Hempel and Chugh, UIST'16) says live sync records run-time traces and forms value-trace equations. It solves one equation per updated attribute by changing exactly one constant, with heuristics for ambiguity. n! is a freeze annotation. n? hints that the solver should prefer to remove that constant. The Draw/Relate/Group tools include Dig Hole, Make Equal and Clean Up. The UIST 2019 'Output-Directed Programming for SVG' paper exists, but I did not open it.

verdicts.name: Apparatus and Recursive Drawing (Toby Schachman)
verdicts.note: The talk page confirms the following. Attributes are expressions that reference other attributes. It is called dataflow and compared to a spreadsheet, with no hidden state and no separate edit and run modes. spread(start,end,step) exists, and separate spreads give a cross product while referencing an existing spread pairs values. The page does not mention Recursive Drawing. Other sources confirm it was Schachman's 2012 ITP thesis, in which a shape can contain itself. recursivedrawing.com had a certificate error when fetched.

verdicts.name: Cuttle (cuttle.xyz)
verdicts.note: The blog post, by Toby Schachman, confirms these points. Cuttle is for CNC cutting (laser cutters, paper cutters, routers). It is both a vector editor and a programming environment. Traditional editors manipulate 'literals', while Cuttle's gestures build a program that is interpreted to make graphics. Reusing shapes inside shapes is likened to functions calling functions. The post does not cover modifiers. Cuttle's scripting docs (cuttle.xyz/learn/getting-started-with-scripting) do: input is a special variable holding geometry from the shape or the previous modifier, modifiers must return geometry, and Rotational Repeat and Outline Stroke were built the same way.

verdicts.name: Bret Victor, 'Drawing Dynamic Visualizations' (talk plus additional notes)
verdicts.note: The addendum confirms the following. The tool lets the artist 'precisely and unambiguously express intent' and does not guess intent. Snapping happens only when a drag starts from a specific point. Tab cycles through overlapping snaps. The artist can snap to the intersection of any two objects. The 'glomp' modifier snaps to an arbitrary, parameterizable position along an object. Program structure is built implicitly by drawing, and steps are generalized by parameterizing them.

verdicts.name: Graphite (graphite.art, formerly graphite.rs)
verdicts.note: The features page confirms that it is in alpha, that the Layers panel and node graph are 'equivalent, interchangeable views', and that parameters can be constants, exposed to the graph, or keyframed (planned, late 2026). It does not name Graphene or Rust. The project's docs (graphite.art/volunteer/guide/graphene) confirm Graphene is the Rust node-graph engine, compiled to WASM in the browser. The Path node for non-destructive edits after a procedural shape is confirmed in the Q3 2024 report (#1676). The Q1 2024 report confirms the vector format moved to an attribute-based design. The points-table detail was not shown on any page I fetched; it matches the codebase but I did not check it here.

verdicts.name: kappa-curves (Adobe Illustrator's Curvature tool) and epsilon-kappa extension
verdicts.note: The paper (Yan, Schiller, Wilensky, Carr, Schaefer, SIGGRAPH 2017) confirms the following. It uses one quadratic per interior control point, and a quadratic has only one curvature maximum. A simple iterative optimization makes the pieces G2 everywhere except at inflections, where they are G1. Loops and cusps cannot appear unless the artist intends them. The paper says it shipped as Illustrator's Curvature tool. Photoshop's Curvature Pen is not mentioned in the paper, but the tool exists. I did not check the epsilon-kappa paper.

verdicts.name: Fitting fair curves: Spiro/Euler spirals (Levien), clothoid sketch fitting (Baran et al.), log-aesthetic curves
verdicts.note: 'Sketching Clothoid Splines Using Shortest Paths' (Baran, Lehtinen, Popovic; Eurographics 2010 / CGF) confirms the method. An overcomplete set of lines, arcs and clothoids is fit to every subsegment. Graph nodes are primitives and edges are transitions with a specified continuity. The shortest path gives the segmentation, which is then refined by nonlinear constrained optimization. I did not check the Levien Spiro or log-aesthetic claims on this page. Log-aesthetic curves do include the logarithmic spiral, but the golden spiral is only one special case of it.

verdicts.name: Slider panels: Tweakpane, lil-gui, Leva
verdicts.note: Tweakpane's docs confirm number, string, boolean, color and point bindings, monitors, folders and tabs, and exportState()/importState(). They say 'Tweakpane doesn't detect changes of bound parameters' and that refresh() forces an update. Change events carry ev.last. lil-gui's README confirms that add() picks the control by type, min and max make a slider, and colors are supported. Its docs site is lil-gui.georgealways.com, which I could not reach. Leva (pmndrs/leva) confirms the useControls hook with input-type inference.

verdicts.name: Observable runtime and Inputs
verdicts.note: The README confirms define(name, inputs, definition) and lazy computation of unobserved variables. A returned promise makes derived variables wait for it to resolve. Generators are pulled on every animation frame. module.derive(specifiers, source) returns a copy of the module with the specified variables replaced by imports. I did not check the Inputs.range and viewof details in the observablehq/inputs repo.

verdicts.name: Figma variables, modes and constraints
verdicts.note: The page confirms six types (color, number, string, boolean, timing, easing), up to 5,000 variables per collection, modes storing one value per variable, and aliasing to a variable of the same type. Number variables bind to dimensions, padding and gap, corner radius, stroke weight, opacity and more. This overview does not mention expressions. Figma's 'Use variables in prototypes' and 'Use expressions in prototypes' articles confirm that expressions are used in prototype Set variable actions. I did not check the constraints part.

verdicts.name: Houdini Wedge TOP (parameter sweeps for review)
verdicts.note: The page exists and supports the claims. The node 'creates work items with varying attribute values' that downstream render TOPs turn into renders you can compare. 'Side by side' is our wording; the page only says the variants can be compared. Range: values are evenly spaced between Start and End, or random within that range when Random Samples is on. Value: either a constant or an expression evaluated per work item; the page's example uses @wedgeindex and ch("wedgecount"). Value List: 'cycles through the values' when there are more wedges than entries. Bracket: center plus or minus an offset, and an odd Wedge Count puts the center value on one work item. Pull reads @attribute references in parameter expressions. Push uses Target Parameter to override that parameter at cook/render time without changing the HIP file. One correction on preview: 'Overwrite Target Parameter on Work Item Selection' really writes the value into the parameter. That triggers recooks and marks the HIP unsaved, and saving keeps the previewed value. The original is stored on the node and restored when the work item is deselected, and Capture/Restore buttons do this by hand. The truncated part of the claim ('Wedges ca...') is consistent with the page: Wedge nodes can be chained or nested, and Preserve Wedge Numbers keeps each level's numbers as arrays.
